phy_ocra.10.0.summary: PAG P1 (Materials) is the practical activity in which you **determine the density** of a variety of objects: **regular solids**, **irregular solids** and **liquids**. Every method comes down to measuring a **mass** with a balance and a **volume** (by measuring dimensions, by **displacement of water**, or with a measuring cylinder) and then using **density = mass / volume**. Examiners test your choice of apparatus, how you reduce uncertainty, how you handle units and how you evaluate the method.

core.p: The OCR practical activity group P1 Materials asks you to determine the densities of a variety of objects, both solid and liquid. It links to P1.1 (the particle model and density) and builds the practical skills assessed in every paper.
bullets: Method 1: **regular solid** (cube, cuboid, cylinder): measure dimensions and calculate volume.
Method 2: **irregular solid** (stone, key, lump of plasticine): find volume by **displacement of water**.
Method 3: **liquid** (water, salt water, oil): measure mass of a known volume.
In each case use **density = mass / volume**.
About 15% of marks across the papers test practical skills, so expect questions on these methods even though they are not written up in the exam.

callouts.p: Density is the mass per unit volume of a material. density (kg/m3) = mass (kg) / volume (m3).

core.p: The equation is rho = m / V, where rho (the Greek letter rho) is density. In the lab you usually measure in grams and cubic centimetres, so the answer comes out in g/cm3; the SI unit is kg/m3.
bullets: **1 g/cm3 = 1000 kg/m3** (water has a density of about 1.0 g/cm3 = 1000 kg/m3).
Rearranged: m = rho x V and V = m / rho.
Objects with a density less than the liquid they are in will **float**; greater density will sink.

callouts.p: To convert g/cm3 to kg/m3 multiply by 1000, not by 100 or 1 000 000.

core.p: Mass is measured with a **top-pan (electronic) balance**, usually with a resolution of 0.01 g or 0.1 g.
bullets: **Zero (tare)** the balance before use so there is no zero error.
Place the object gently in the centre of the pan and wait for the reading to settle.
For a liquid, tare with the empty measuring cylinder on the pan, then add the liquid, so the balance reads the liquid's mass only.
Make sure the object is dry; water on the surface adds mass.

callouts.p: Taring removes the mass of the container in one step and avoids subtracting two readings, which would combine their uncertainties.

core.p: For a cube, cuboid or cylinder you can calculate the volume from its dimensions. Choose a measuring instrument whose **resolution** suits the size being measured.
bullets: Measure length, width and height with a **ruler** (resolution 1 mm) or, for small objects, **vernier callipers** (0.1 mm) or a **micrometer** (0.01 mm).
Measure each dimension **several times at different places** and take the mean, in case the block is not perfectly regular.
Cuboid: V = length x width x height.
Cylinder: V = pi x r squared x h, where r is half the measured diameter.
Measure the mass on a balance, then calculate rho = m / V.

callouts.p: The smallest dimension has the largest percentage uncertainty, so it matters most to measure it with a high-resolution instrument.

core.p: An irregular object cannot be measured with a ruler, so its volume is found by the volume of water it **displaces** (pushes aside) when fully submerged.
bullets: Fill a **eureka (displacement) can** with water until it runs out of the spout; wait until it stops dripping.
Put an empty **measuring cylinder** under the spout.
Lower the object in gently on a thread so it is **completely submerged** and does not splash.
Collect all the water that overflows; its volume equals the **volume of the object**.
Alternatively: part-fill a measuring cylinder, read the volume, add the object, read again. Volume of object = final reading - initial reading.
Measure the mass of the dry object (before putting it in water) and calculate rho = m / V.

callouts.p: If the object floats it is not fully submerged, so the displaced volume is too small. Push it under with a thin pin or attach a sinker of known volume.

core.p: For a liquid you measure the mass of a known volume.
bullets: Place an empty measuring cylinder on the balance and **tare** it to zero.
Pour in liquid up to a chosen volume, for example 50 cm3, reading at the **bottom of the meniscus**.
Read the mass of the liquid from the balance.
Calculate rho = m / V.
Add more liquid (for example in 10 cm3 steps), recording total volume and mass each time; plot **mass against volume**. The **gradient** is the density.
Using a larger volume reduces the percentage uncertainty in the volume reading.

callouts.p: A graph of mass (y) against volume (x) is a straight line through the origin; gradient = mass / volume = density. Using a graph averages out random errors.

core.p: Water forms a curved surface called a **meniscus** in a narrow cylinder. Readings must be taken consistently to avoid systematic error.
bullets: Place the cylinder on a **flat, level surface**.
Read from the **bottom of the meniscus** for water (top for mercury, not used in schools).
Have your **eye level with the meniscus** to avoid **parallax error**.
Choose the smallest cylinder that holds the volume, because it has the finest scale divisions (better resolution).

callouts.p: An error caused by reading a scale from an angle rather than looking straight at it, so the reading appears higher or lower than it really is.

core.p: In density practicals you are usually measuring rather than changing a variable, but you should still identify sources of error and control conditions.
bullets: **Independent variable** (if comparing): the material or object.
**Dependent variable**: the density (calculated from mass and volume).
**Control**: temperature of the liquid (density changes slightly with temperature), same balance throughout, same reading technique.
Make the object **dry** before weighing and remove **air bubbles** clinging to it in the water.

core.p: Evaluation questions ask you to identify errors and suggest improvements. Know the difference between random and systematic errors.
bullets: **Random error**: readings scattered either side of the true value (e.g. judging the meniscus). Reduce by **repeating and taking a mean**.

**Systematic error**: every reading wrong by the same amount or proportion (e.g. balance not zeroed, always reading the top of the meniscus). Cannot be reduced by repeats; fix the technique or recalibrate.
**Zero error**: an instrument reads a value when it should read zero. A type of systematic error.
Eureka can errors: water left in the spout, drips not collected, water clinging to the measuring cylinder, splashing.
**Uncertainty** in a reading is about half the resolution (or half the range of repeats).
Percentage uncertainty = (uncertainty / measured value) x 100.

core.p: Mark schemes reward these words used precisely.
bullets: **Accurate**: close to the true value.
**Precise**: repeated measurements are close to each other (little spread).
**Resolution**: the smallest change an instrument can detect (e.g. 1 cm3 on a 100 cm3 cylinder).
**Repeatable**: the same person, same method, same equipment gets similar results.
**Reproducible**: a different person or method gets similar results.
Compare your density with a data book value to judge accuracy, and calculate percentage difference.

callouts.p: Readings can be very close together (precise) but all wrong because of a systematic error (not accurate).

core.p: This is a low-hazard practical, but you should still be able to make a sensible risk assessment.
bullets: Wipe up spilled water so nobody slips and so the electronic balance is not damaged.
Lower heavy objects into glassware gently on a thread so the glass does not crack.
Keep liquids (especially oil or salt solution) away from electrical sockets.
Handle sharp-edged metal blocks carefully.

core.h: Typical results and what they tell you
core.p: Knowing typical densities lets you spot an answer that is clearly wrong, for example a stone with a density less than water that still sank.
bullets: Water about 1.0 g/cm3; cooking oil about 0.9 g/cm3; salt water about 1.1 g/cm3.
Aluminium about 2.7 g/cm3; iron/steel about 7.9 g/cm3; copper about 8.9 g/cm3.
Typical rocks about 2.5 to 3 g/cm3; wood about 0.5 to 0.8 g/cm3.
If your value is far from the expected one, check units, a missed decimal place, or whether all the object was submerged.

callouts.p: An object that sinks in water must have a density greater than 1 g/cm3; if your calculation says otherwise, there is an error.

analogy.p: Density is like how heavily a suitcase is packed. Two suitcases may be the same size (volume) but the one stuffed with books has more mass in the same space, so it is denser. Measuring density is like weighing the suitcase and measuring its size, then dividing. Displacement is like getting into a full bath: the water that spills over is exactly the space your body takes up. Where it breaks down: a suitcase has empty gaps you can see, whereas the density of a material is an average over particles too small to see, and a person in a bath is not usually fully submerged.

An object with a simple geometric shape whose volume can be calculated from measured dimensions.
An object with no simple shape, so its volume must be found by displacement.
The pushing aside of liquid by a submerged object; the volume of liquid displaced equals the volume of the object.
A can with a spout near the top, filled to the spout so that water displaced by an object flows out to be collected.
The curved surface of a liquid in a narrow container; water readings are taken from the bottom of the curve.
An error from reading a scale at an angle instead of with the eye level with the reading.
The smallest change in a quantity that an instrument can detect.
When an instrument gives a non-zero reading when the true value is zero; a type of systematic error.
An error that makes readings vary unpredictably around the true value; reduced by repeating and averaging.
An error that shifts all readings by the same amount or in the same direction; not reduced by repeating.
The interval within which the true value is expected to lie, often half the resolution or half the range of repeats.
How close a measurement is to the true value.
How close repeated measurements are to each other.
An instrument for measuring small lengths and diameters to a resolution of about 0.1 mm.

mistakes.w: Density = volume / mass.
mistakes.r: Density = mass / volume.

mistakes.w: Converting 2.7 g/cm3 to 2.7 kg/m3 or 270 kg/m3.
mistakes.r: Multiply by 1000: 2.7 g/cm3 = 2700 kg/m3.

mistakes.w: Read the top of the meniscus.
mistakes.r: Read the bottom of the meniscus with the eye level with it.

mistakes.w: Repeat the readings to remove the zero error.
mistakes.r: Repeats reduce random error; a zero error is systematic and is removed by zeroing (taring) the balance.

mistakes.w: Drop the stone into the eureka can.
mistakes.r: Lower it gently on a thread so no water splashes out and is lost.

mistakes.w: The volume of the stone is the final reading on the measuring cylinder.
mistakes.r: Volume = final reading - initial reading (unless using a eureka can and an empty cylinder).

mistakes.w: Use a ruler to measure the thickness of a coin.
mistakes.r: Use vernier callipers or a micrometer because they have a finer resolution, reducing percentage uncertainty.

mistakes.w: Precise means the answer is correct.
mistakes.r: Precise means repeat readings are close together; accurate means close to the true value.

exam.q: State the equation linking density, mass and volume.
model: density = mass / volume
exam.tip: Learn it in words and symbols (rho = m / V).

exam.q: Name a piece of apparatus used to measure the volume of an irregular stone.
model: Eureka (displacement) can and measuring cylinder (or measuring cylinder alone).
exam.tip: Name both parts for a two-mark version.

exam.q: Explain why the student should place her eye level with the water surface when reading a measuring cylinder.
model: To avoid parallax error.
So the reading is not too high or too low / the volume is accurate.
exam.tip: Name the error and its effect.

exam.q: A metal block has mass 270 g and measures 5.0 cm x 4.0 cm x 5.0 cm. Calculate its density in g/cm3.
exam.tip: Show the volume calculation for the first mark.

exam.q: Convert 2.7 g/cm3 into kg/m3.
Describe how to determine the density of an irregularly shaped stone.
model: Measure the mass of the dry stone on a zeroed top-pan balance.
Fill a eureka can to the spout and place an empty measuring cylinder under the spout.
Lower the stone in on a thread until fully submerged and collect the displaced water; read its volume at the bottom of the meniscus.
Calculate density = mass / volume, and repeat to find a mean.
exam.tip: Mass, volume, calculation, repeat.

exam.q: A student finds the volume of a stone using a eureka can. Suggest two reasons why her value for the volume may be too small.
model: Water remaining in the spout / drips not collected.
Water clinging to the inside of the beaker or splashing out; or stone not fully submerged.
exam.tip: Think about where displaced water could go other than the cylinder.

exam.q: Describe how to determine the density of cooking oil. Include how you would make your result as accurate as possible.
model: Place an empty measuring cylinder on a balance and tare to zero.
Add oil to a measured volume, reading at eye level at the bottom of the meniscus, and record the mass.
Repeat for several volumes and plot mass against volume.
Density = gradient of the line; a larger volume / graph reduces percentage uncertainty.
exam.tip: A graph method earns credit for accuracy.

exam.q: Explain the difference between a random error and a systematic error, using examples from a density experiment.
model: A random error causes readings to scatter unpredictably about the true value,
e.g. slight differences in judging the meniscus each time; reduced by repeating and averaging.
A systematic error shifts all readings the same way,
e.g. balance not zeroed (zero error); reduced by correcting the technique or instrument, not by repeats.
exam.tip: Definition plus example for each type.

exam.q: Plan an investigation to compare the densities of a metal cube, a stone and a sample of salt water. Explain how you would obtain accurate and precise results.
model: Cube: measure each side with vernier callipers at several places, calculate mean side and V = side cubed.
Stone: find volume by displacement using a eureka can and measuring cylinder, lowering on a thread.
Salt water: tare a measuring cylinder on the balance, add a measured volume, record the mass.
Measure all masses on a zeroed top-pan balance; dry objects before weighing.
Read volumes at eye level at the bottom of the meniscus to avoid parallax error.
Repeat each measurement and calculate a mean density, rho = m / V; compare with data values to judge accuracy.
exam.tip: Level of response: give a method for all three and specific accuracy/precision steps.

worked.q: A brass cylinder has a diameter of 2.00 cm, length 5.00 cm and mass 132 g. Calculate its density in g/cm3 and kg/m3.
steps: V = pi x r squared x h = 3.14 x 1.00 x 1.00 x 5.00 = 15.7 cm3.

worked.q: A measuring cylinder contains 40 cm3 of water. A stone of mass 65 g is lowered in and the reading rises to 66 cm3. Calculate the density of the stone and state whether it will sink in salt water of density 1.1 g/cm3.
worked.ans: 2.5 g/cm3; it sinks because it is denser than the salt water.

worked.q: A student measures 50.0 cm3 of liquid and gets a mass of 46 g. The measuring cylinder has a resolution of 1 cm3. Calculate the density and the percentage uncertainty in the volume.
steps: Uncertainty in volume = half the resolution = 0.5 cm3.
worked.ans: 0.92 g/cm3 with about 1% uncertainty in volume; using a larger volume would reduce this further.

phy_ocra.10.1.summary: PAG P2 (Forces) centres on investigating the **relationship between force and extension** for a spring. You hang known masses from a spring, measure the **extension** with a metre rule, and plot **force against extension**. For a spring obeying **Hooke's law** the graph is a straight line through the origin up to the **limit of proportionality**; its **gradient is the spring constant k** (F = k x) and the **area under the line is the elastic potential energy stored** (E = 1/2 k x squared). Examiners test the method, variables, accuracy and the analysis of the graph.

core.p: The OCR practical activity group P2 Forces develops skills in measuring forces and their effects. The key investigation is how the extension of a spring depends on the force applied, linked to the spec content on elastic and plastic deformation and Hooke's law.
bullets: Investigate the **force-extension** relationship for a spring.
Use the results to find the **spring constant** k from the gradient.
Identify the **limit of proportionality** where the line stops being straight.
Calculate the **energy stored** using the area under the graph or E = 1/2 k x squared.
Measure forces with a **newtonmeter** and use W = m x g to find the weight of hanging masses.

callouts.p: The extension of an elastic object is directly proportional to the force applied, provided the limit of proportionality is not exceeded. F = k x.

core.p: Three equations are needed to analyse this practical.
bullets: **Weight: W = m x g**, where g = 9.8 N/kg (OCR may use 10 N/kg in some questions). A 100 g mass has a weight of about 1 N.
**Hooke's law: F = k x**, force (N) = spring constant (N/m) x extension (m).
**Elastic potential energy: E = 1/2 k x squared**, energy (J) = 0.5 x spring constant (N/m) x extension squared (m2). Valid only up to the limit of proportionality.
**Extension = current length - original (unstretched) length.**

callouts.p: Always subtract the original length. Plotting total length gives a line that does not go through the origin.

core.p: A simple setup gives reliable results if it is arranged carefully.
bullets: **Clamp stand**, boss and clamp to hold the spring.
The **spring** and a **mass hanger** with slotted masses (usually 100 g each, weight about 1 N).
A **metre rule** held vertically by a second clamp, close to the spring.
A **pointer** (a splint or pin) fixed to the bottom of the spring to read the scale sharply.
A **G-clamp** or heavy weight on the base so the stand cannot topple.

core.p: Follow a clear step-by-step method; this is exactly what a six-mark planning question asks for.
bullets: 1. Clamp the spring and ruler so the ruler is **vertical** and its zero lines up with the top of the spring (or note the starting reading).
2. Record the **original length** (or pointer position) with no load, eye level with the pointer.
3. Add one 100 g mass (about 1 N). Wait for the spring to stop moving, then record the new pointer reading.
4. Calculate extension = new reading - original reading.
5. Repeat, adding one mass at a time, up to about 8 to 10 masses.
6. Remove the masses one at a time and record the readings again to check whether the spring returns to its original length (has the **elastic limit** been passed?).
7. Calculate the mean extension for each force and plot force (or extension) against the other.

callouts.p: Taking readings while adding and then removing masses gives repeat readings and shows whether the deformation was elastic.

core.p: Identify variables precisely; questions often ask for one example of each.
bullets: **Independent variable**: the force (weight of masses added).
**Dependent variable**: the extension of the spring.
**Control variables**: the same spring throughout, the same ruler position, the same reading technique, room temperature.
Force is changed in equal steps (e.g. 1 N) to give evenly spread points on the graph.

core.p: Most errors in this practical come from reading the ruler.
bullets: Read with your **eye level with the pointer** to avoid **parallax error**.
Make sure the ruler is **vertical** (use a set square against the bench).
Wait until the spring is **stationary** before reading.
Use a **fine pointer** attached to the bottom of the spring to read to the nearest millimetre.
Check the ruler has not been knocked between readings; a moved ruler causes a **systematic error**.

callouts.p: The smallest change an instrument can measure. A metre rule has a resolution of 1 mm.

core.p: Plot **force on the y-axis and extension on the x-axis** so the gradient is the spring constant (some questions plot it the other way round; then the gradient is 1/k).
bullets: Choose scales that use **more than half the grid**.
Plot points accurately with small crosses.
Draw a **line of best fit**: a straight line through the origin for the proportional section.
Where the points start to curve away, the spring has passed its **limit of proportionality**.
Points that do not fit the pattern are **anomalous**; circle them, repeat the reading if possible, and leave them out of the best-fit line.

callouts.p: A straight line through the origin shows that extension is directly proportional to force: doubling the force doubles the extension.

core.p: The gradient of the straight part of a force-extension graph is the spring constant k.
bullets: Draw a large triangle on the straight section of the line.
k = change in force / change in extension.
Extension must be in **metres** to give k in N/m.
A **stiffer** spring has a larger k: a steeper force-extension line.
Alternatively calculate k = F / x for each reading and take a mean (only for points in the linear region).

callouts.p: An extension of 4.0 cm is 0.040 m. Forgetting this gives k 100 times too small.

core.h: Energy stored and the area under the graph
core.p: Work is done stretching the spring, and this energy is stored as **elastic potential energy**. On a force-extension graph, the **area under the line** equals the work done (energy stored).
bullets: For the linear region the area is a triangle: E = 1/2 x F x x.
Since F = k x, this becomes **E = 1/2 k x squared**.
Beyond the limit of proportionality, the area must be found by counting squares; the equation no longer applies.
If the spring is deformed **plastically**, not all the work done is recovered: some is dissipated (heating the spring).

callouts.p: Area = force (N) x extension (m), giving joules. Check axis units before counting squares.

core.p: The practical also shows the difference between elastic and inelastic (plastic) behaviour.
bullets: **Elastic deformation**: the object returns to its original shape and length when the force is removed.
**Plastic (inelastic) deformation**: the object does not return to its original shape; it is permanently stretched.
The **elastic limit** is the point beyond which deformation becomes plastic; for a spring it is close to the limit of proportionality.
Stretching needs **more than one force**: the weight pulls down and the clamp pulls up.

core.p: Evaluation questions ask you to spot errors and suggest how to improve the method.
bullets: **Random error**: reading the pointer slightly differently each time; reduce by repeating (loading and unloading) and taking a mean.
**Systematic error**: ruler not vertical or zero not aligned (zero error); every extension is off by the same amount. Fix the setup.
Masses on hanger may not be exactly 100 g; check them on a balance.
Small extensions have high percentage uncertainty; use a softer spring or larger forces to get larger extensions.
Use more data points near the limit of proportionality to locate it more precisely.

core.p: The main hazards come from falling masses and a spring that may snap.
bullets: Clamp the stand to the bench or use a counterweight so it cannot topple.
Do not stand with feet directly under the masses; place a tray or soft mat underneath.
Wear **eye protection**: an over-stretched spring can snap or fly off.
Do not overload the spring far beyond its limit.

callouts.p: Safety marks need both: the hazard (masses falling on feet) and how to reduce it (tray underneath, stand clamped).

analogy.p: A spring in its linear region is like a fair shopkeeper who always charges the same price per item: each extra newton of pull buys exactly the same extra stretch. The price per item is the spring constant k: a stiff spring is an expensive shop (lots of newtons per metre). Go past the limit of proportionality and the shop starts changing its prices, so the simple rule no longer works. Where it breaks down: a shop does not get permanently damaged by big orders, whereas a spring stretched past its elastic limit stays longer for ever.

terms.d: A push or pull acting on an object, measured in newtons (N).
The force acting on an object due to gravity; W = m x g.
The force per kilogram exerted by gravity; about 9.8 N/kg on Earth.
The increase in length of a spring: stretched length minus original length.
Extension is directly proportional to the applied force, up to the limit of proportionality: F = k x.
The force needed per unit extension of a spring, in N/m; the gradient of a force-extension graph.
The point beyond which force and extension are no longer directly proportional.
The maximum force beyond which an object will not return to its original shape.
A change of shape that is fully reversed when the force is removed.
A change of shape that remains after the force is removed.
Energy stored in a stretched or compressed object; E = 1/2 k x squared in the linear region.
Two quantities that increase in the same ratio; a straight-line graph through the origin.
A spring balance calibrated to measure force in newtons.
An error caused by reading a scale at an angle rather than at eye level.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the other results.
The variable you deliberately change: here, the force on the spring.
The variable you measure: here, the extension.

mistakes.w: Plotting the total length instead of the extension.
mistakes.r: Extension = stretched length - original length; plot extension.

mistakes.w: The mass on the spring is 300 g so the force is 300 N.
mistakes.r: Convert to kg and use W = m g: 0.300 x 9.8 = 2.9 N.

mistakes.w: Hooke's law says force is proportional to length.
mistakes.r: Force is directly proportional to extension, up to the limit of proportionality.

mistakes.w: The limit of proportionality is where the graph starts.
mistakes.r: It is the point where the straight line starts to curve.

mistakes.w: k = extension / force.
mistakes.r: k = force / extension (gradient of force against extension).

mistakes.w: Repeating readings removes the zero error.
mistakes.r: Repeating reduces random error; a zero error is systematic and must be corrected in the setup.

mistakes.w: E = 1/2 k x squared works for the whole graph.
mistakes.r: It only applies while the spring obeys Hooke's law; beyond that, use the area under the curve.

mistakes.w: Using extension in cm in F = k x.
mistakes.r: Convert to metres to give k in N/m and energy in J.

exam.q: State the independent variable in an experiment to investigate how the extension of a spring depends on the force applied.
model: The force (weight) applied to the spring.
exam.tip: The variable you change.

exam.q: Describe how the extension of the spring is calculated from the ruler readings.
model: Extension = new length (reading) - original length (reading).
exam.tip: Mention the original unstretched length.

exam.q: Suggest two ways to make the ruler readings more accurate.
model: Read with eye level with the pointer to avoid parallax.
Make sure the ruler is vertical / use a pointer / wait for the spring to stop moving.
exam.tip: Specific actions, not just 'be careful'.

exam.q: A spring extends by 0.050 m when a force of 2.0 N is applied. Calculate the spring constant.
model: k = 40 N/m
exam.tip: Rearrange F = k x.

exam.q: Calculate the elastic potential energy stored in the spring in the previous question.
model: E = 1/2 x 40 x 0.050 squared
exam.tip: Square the extension before multiplying.

exam.q: State how the graph shows that the spring obeys Hooke's law.
model: The graph is a straight line
that passes through the origin.
exam.tip: Both points needed.

exam.q: Explain what happened to a spring which did not return to its original length after the masses were removed.
model: The spring was stretched beyond its elastic limit.
It was deformed plastically / inelastically, so it is permanently extended.
exam.tip: Use 'elastic limit'.

exam.q: Explain how the spring constant can be found from a graph of force against extension.
model: Calculate the gradient of the straight (linear) part of the line.
Gradient = change in force / change in extension = k.
exam.tip: Use a large triangle.

exam.q: Identify one hazard in this experiment and explain how to reduce the risk.
model: Masses could fall on feet / stand could topple.
Place a tray or cushion underneath and clamp the stand to the bench.
exam.tip: Hazard plus control.

exam.q: Describe a method to investigate the relationship between force and extension for a spring, and explain how you would use your results to find the spring constant.
model: Hang the spring from a clamp stand with a vertical metre rule alongside; record the original length with a pointer at eye level.
Add 100 g (about 1 N) masses one at a time, recording the pointer reading after the spring stops moving.
Calculate extension = reading - original reading for each force.
Repeat by removing masses / repeating the experiment and take means; identify anomalies.
Plot force (y) against extension (x) and draw a line of best fit.
The gradient of the straight section is k; check that the line passes through the origin to confirm Hooke's law.
exam.tip: Level of response: method, variables/accuracy and analysis all needed for level 3.

worked.q: A student adds masses to a spring of original length 20.0 cm. With 400 g hanging, the length is 28.0 cm. Calculate the force, the extension and the spring constant (g = 9.8 N/kg).
Using the spring above, calculate the energy stored when the extension is 0.080 m. State one assumption.
steps: E = 1/2 x k x x squared.
worked.ans: 0.16 J, assuming the spring has not passed its limit of proportionality.

worked.q: A force-extension graph is a straight line through the origin up to 5.0 N at 0.10 m, then curves. Find k and the energy stored at 0.10 m from the graph.
steps: Gradient of the straight section = 5.0 / 0.10 = 50 N/m.
Area under the line up to 0.10 m is a triangle: 1/2 x 5.0 x 0.10.
worked.ans: k = 50 N/m; energy stored = 0.25 J.

phy_ocra.10.2.summary: PAG P3 (Motion) is about measuring **speed** and **acceleration** in the lab and using them to investigate how motion depends on force and mass. You measure distances with a rule and times with a stopwatch or, far more accurately, with **light gates** and a data logger, then use **speed = distance / time** and **acceleration = change in velocity / time**. The classic investigation pulls a trolley with a falling mass to show that **acceleration is proportional to resultant force** and **inversely proportional to mass** (F = m a), and examiners test the method, error reduction and graph analysis.

core.p: The OCR practical activity group P3 Motion develops techniques for measuring motion and links to the P2 Forces content on speed, acceleration and Newton's second law.
bullets: Measure the **speed** of a moving object, e.g. a trolley, a toy car or a person walking.
Measure the **acceleration** of a trolley down a ramp or pulled by a falling mass.
Investigate how acceleration depends on **resultant force** (constant mass).
Investigate how acceleration depends on **mass** (constant force).
Choose between **stopwatch**, **light gates**, a **ticker timer** or **video analysis**, and justify the choice.

callouts.p: The rate of change of velocity. acceleration (m/s2) = change in velocity (m/s) / time taken (s).

core.p: Every calculation in this practical uses one of these equations, all given on the OCR equation sheet or required to be recalled.
bullets: **speed = distance / time** (v = d / t), units m/s.
**acceleration = change in velocity / time** (a = (v - u) / t), units m/s2.
**v squared - u squared = 2 a s**, useful when two light gates are a known distance s apart.
**Force = mass x acceleration** (F = m a), Newton's second law.
**Weight = mass x g** (W = m g) for the falling mass that provides the pulling force; g = 9.8 N/kg.

core.p: To measure average speed you need a distance and the time taken to cover it.
bullets: Mark out a measured distance (e.g. 1.00 m) with a metre rule or tape measure.
Time the object with a **stopwatch**: start as it passes the first mark, stop at the second.
Human **reaction time** (about 0.2 s) causes large errors over short times, so use long distances or light gates.
A **light gate** measures the time a card of known length takes to pass through the beam; speed = card length / time.
Repeat several times and calculate a mean.

callouts.p: Light gates remove human reaction time, record to a resolution of about 0.001 s, and calculate speed automatically, so results are more accurate and more precise.

core.p: A light gate has a light source on one side and a sensor on the other. When an object breaks the beam the data logger times how long the beam is blocked.
bullets: Fit a card of measured length (e.g. 10.0 cm) to the trolley so it passes through the gate.
Speed at the gate = card length / time beam blocked.
**Two light gates**: measure the speed at each gate (u and v) and the time between them, then a = (v - u) / t.
**Single gate, double card** (two segments): the logger measures the speed for each segment and the time between them to calculate acceleration.
Line the gate up so the card, not the wheels or string, breaks the beam.

callouts.p: Measure the card length with a ruler and enter it into the data logger; an error here is a systematic error in every speed.

core.p: A trolley released from rest on a ramp accelerates because a component of its weight acts down the slope.
bullets: Set up a ramp and place two light gates a measured distance apart.
Release the trolley from the **same starting point** each time, **without pushing**.
Record u, v and the time between gates; calculate a = (v - u) / t, or use v squared - u squared = 2 a s.
Change the height of the ramp to investigate how angle affects acceleration (control the starting position and trolley mass).
Repeat each height three times and take the mean.

core.h: Investigating force and acceleration (F = m a)
core.p: A trolley on a runway is pulled by a string passing over a pulley to a hanging mass. The weight of the hanging mass provides the accelerating force.
bullets: Independent variable: the **pulling force** (weight of hanging masses).
Dependent variable: the **acceleration** of the trolley.
Control: the **total mass of the system** (trolley + hanging masses).
To keep total mass constant, start with all the slotted masses on the trolley and **move them one at a time from the trolley to the hanger**.
For each force, release the trolley from rest and measure acceleration with light gates.
Plot acceleration against force: a **straight line through the origin** shows a is directly proportional to F.

callouts.p: If you just add masses to the hanger, the total mass being accelerated increases too, so you change two variables at once and the test is not fair.

core.p: To find how acceleration depends on mass, keep the pulling force constant and change the mass of the trolley.
bullets: Keep the same hanging mass (constant force).
Add masses to the trolley (e.g. stacking 0.25 kg blocks) and measure the acceleration for each.
As mass increases, acceleration decreases.
A graph of a against 1/m is a straight line through the origin: **a is inversely proportional to m**.
The gradient of the a against 1/m graph equals the force F.

core.p: Friction acts against the motion, so the resultant force on the trolley is less than the weight of the hanging mass. This gives a systematic error.
bullets: Tilt the runway slightly until the trolley, given a small push, rolls down at a **constant speed** (equal gaps on a ticker tape or equal light gate times).
Now a component of weight balances friction, so the **resultant force** equals the pulling force.
Without compensation, the a-F graph is a straight line that **does not pass through the origin**: it cuts the force axis at the value of the friction force.
Use low-friction trolleys or an air track to reduce friction further.

callouts.p: F = m a uses the resultant force. Friction reduces the resultant force, so acceleration is smaller than predicted.

core.p: You may be asked to compare methods and justify the best one.
bullets: **Stopwatch**: cheap and simple, but reaction time makes it inaccurate for short times.
**Ticker timer**: makes dots at fixed intervals (often 50 per second) on a tape; dot spacing shows speed, increasing spacing shows acceleration.
**Video analysis**: film the motion against a scale and step through frames; good for fast motion, needs a known frame rate.
**Light gates with data logger**: most accurate and precise, automatic calculation, but expensive and needs careful alignment.

core.p: Graph skills are tested heavily in motion practicals.
bullets: **Distance-time graph**: gradient = speed.
**Velocity-time graph**: gradient = acceleration; area under the line = distance travelled.
**Acceleration-force graph**: straight line through origin shows direct proportion; gradient = 1 / mass.
Draw a line of best fit and ignore anomalous points; use a large triangle for gradients.
A line that misses the origin suggests a **systematic error** such as unbalanced friction or a zero error.

callouts.p: Since a = F / m, the gradient of an a against F graph is 1/m. So mass = 1 / gradient.

core.p: Evaluation answers must link a specific error to a specific improvement.
bullets: **Random errors**: variation in release, timing by hand. Reduce by repeating and taking a mean.
**Systematic errors**: friction, wrong card length, distance between gates measured wrongly. Correct the method.
Release the trolley from rest each time, not pushing; use a fixed start line or a block.
Make sure the string is **parallel to the runway** and the pulley turns freely.
Make the distance between light gates large to reduce the percentage uncertainty in s.

core.p: Moving trolleys and falling masses are the main hazards.
bullets: Put a **buffer or box** at the end of the runway to stop the trolley falling off the bench.
Place a **tray or cushion** under the hanging masses so they do not land on feet.
Keep the falling distance short and do not use large masses.
Keep cables from light gates tidy so nobody trips.

callouts.p: State the hazard (trolley falls off bench) and the control (buffer at end of runway) to get both marks.

analogy.p: Pushing an empty shopping trolley harder makes it speed up faster: double the push, double the acceleration (a proportional to F). Fill it with heavy shopping and the same push gives much less acceleration (a inversely proportional to m). Moving masses from trolley to hanger is like a friend taking items out of the trolley and using them to pull harder, so the total load stays the same. Where it breaks down: a real shopping trolley has lots of friction, which is exactly what the tilted runway is designed to cancel out.

terms.d: Distance travelled per unit time; a scalar, measured in m/s.
Speed in a given direction; a vector, measured in m/s.
The rate of change of velocity: a = (v - u) / t, in m/s2.
The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object combined.
The acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force on it and inversely proportional to its mass: F = m a.
A sensor that detects when a beam of light is broken and records the time, used with a data logger to measure speed.
A card of known length attached to a trolley that blocks the light gate beam; speed = length / time blocked.
A device that records and processes readings from sensors such as light gates automatically.
A device that marks dots on a paper tape at regular time intervals so motion can be analysed.
The time between seeing an event and responding to it; about 0.2 s, a source of error when using a stopwatch.
A force that opposes motion between surfaces in contact.
A runway tilted just enough that a trolley rolls at constant speed, so friction is balanced.
When one quantity doubles, the other doubles; a straight-line graph through the origin.
When one quantity doubles, the other halves.
An unpredictable error that causes readings to spread around the true value; reduced by repeating.
An error that shifts every reading in the same direction; reduced by improving the method or equipment.

mistakes.w: Add masses to the hanger to increase the force.
mistakes.r: Move masses from the trolley to the hanger so the total mass stays constant.

mistakes.w: Acceleration = velocity / time.
mistakes.r: Acceleration = change in velocity / time taken.

mistakes.w: Light gates are better because they are more reliable.
mistakes.r: Light gates remove human reaction time and have a higher resolution, so readings are more accurate.

mistakes.w: The force on the trolley is the mass on the hanger, e.g. 100 g = 100 N.
mistakes.r: Force = weight = m g = 0.100 x 9.8 = 0.98 N.

mistakes.w: The a-F line does not go through the origin because of random error.
mistakes.r: It is a systematic error, usually friction not being compensated.

mistakes.w: Speed at the light gate = distance between gates / time blocked.
mistakes.r: Speed at one gate = length of card / time the beam is blocked.

mistakes.w: Heavier trolleys accelerate more because they have more weight.
mistakes.r: For a constant pulling force, greater mass means smaller acceleration (a = F / m).

mistakes.w: Repeat readings make the results more accurate.
mistakes.r: Repeats reduce the effect of random errors and improve precision; they do not remove systematic error.

exam.q: State the equation linking acceleration, change in velocity and time.
model: acceleration = change in velocity / time
exam.tip: Write it in words or as a = (v - u) / t.

exam.q: Give one reason why light gates give more accurate results than a stopwatch.
model: They remove human reaction time error / have a higher resolution.
exam.tip: Be specific: 'reaction time'.

exam.q: A 0.050 m card blocks a light gate for 0.025 s. Calculate the speed of the trolley.
exam.tip: Speed = card length / time.

exam.q: A trolley's speed rises from 0.40 m/s to 1.20 m/s in 0.50 s. Calculate its acceleration.
exam.tip: Change in velocity first.

exam.q: Explain why masses are moved from the trolley to the hanger, rather than simply added to the hanger.
model: This keeps the total mass of the system constant.
So only the force changes and it is a fair test.
exam.tip: Name the control variable.

exam.q: A graph of acceleration against force does not pass through the origin. Suggest a reason and how to correct it.
model: Friction acts on the trolley so the resultant force is less than the weight of the hanging mass.
Tilt the runway until the trolley rolls at constant speed (friction compensated).
exam.tip: Identify a systematic error.

exam.q: Two light gates are 0.60 m apart. A trolley passes the first at 0.30 m/s and the second at 0.90 m/s. Calculate its acceleration.
model: v squared - u squared = 2 a s
exam.tip: Higher: use the equation sheet.

exam.q: State one hazard in the trolley experiment and how to reduce the risk.
model: Trolley falls off the end of the bench / hanging masses fall on feet.
Place a buffer at the end of the runway / put a tray underneath the masses.
exam.tip: Hazard and control.

exam.q: Describe how to measure the acceleration of a trolley rolling down a ramp using light gates.
model: Fix an interrupt card of measured length to the trolley.
Place two light gates a measured distance apart on the ramp, connected to a data logger.
Release the trolley from rest from the same point; record the speed at each gate and the time between gates.
Calculate a = (v - u) / t; repeat and calculate a mean.
exam.tip: Include release from rest and repeats.

exam.q: Plan an investigation to show how the acceleration of a trolley depends on the resultant force acting on it. Include how you would make your results valid and how you would analyse them.
model: Trolley on a runway connected by string over a pulley to a mass hanger; light gates and data logger measure acceleration.
Compensate for friction by tilting the runway until the trolley rolls at constant speed.
Start with slotted masses on the trolley and move them one at a time to the hanger so the total mass stays constant.
Force = weight of hanging masses = m g; release from rest at the same point each time.
Repeat each force three times and calculate mean acceleration; check for anomalies.
Plot acceleration against force; a straight line through the origin shows a is directly proportional to F, gradient = 1 / total mass.
exam.tip: Level of response: setup, control of variables, and analysis are all needed for level 3.

worked.q: A trolley has a double interrupt card with two 5.0 cm segments. The first segment blocks the gate for 0.10 s and the second for 0.050 s. The time between the start of each segment is 0.20 s. Calculate the acceleration.
In the force investigation, the total mass of trolley plus masses is 0.80 kg. A hanging mass of 0.040 kg is used (g = 9.8 N/kg). Predict the acceleration, assuming friction is compensated.
steps: The whole system (0.80 kg) accelerates together.
worked.ans: About 0.49 m/s2

worked.q: A student's graph of acceleration (y) against force (x) has a gradient of 2.0 (m/s2 per N) and cuts the force axis at 0.10 N. Find the mass of the system and interpret the intercept.
steps: a = F / m, so gradient = 1 / m.
The intercept at 0.10 N means no acceleration until the force exceeds 0.10 N.
This is the friction force that has not been compensated (a systematic error).
worked.ans: Mass = 0.50 kg; friction is about 0.10 N and the runway should be tilted to compensate.

phy_ocra.10.3.summary: PAG P4 is the group of practicals where you **measure the speed, frequency and wavelength of waves** and check that they fit the **wave equation v = f x λ**. The classic set-ups are water waves in a **ripple tank**, waves on a **stretched string** driven by a vibration generator, and the **speed of sound** in air (or in a solid). Examiners test the method, the measurements, the sources of error and how to make the results more accurate.

core.p: Every wave carries energy from place to place without transferring matter. To describe a wave we measure how fast it travels, how many waves pass each second and how long one wave is. PAG P4 asks you to make these measurements for real waves and link them with the wave equation.
bullets: **Wave speed (v)**: distance travelled by the wave per second, in m/s.
**Frequency (f)**: number of waves passing a point each second, in hertz (Hz).
**Wavelength (λ)**: distance from one point on a wave to the same point on the next wave (e.g. crest to crest), in metres.
**Period (T)**: time for one complete wave to pass, T = 1 / f.
You should be able to measure each quantity directly and also calculate one from the other two.
The same equation works for water waves, waves on strings, sound and light.

callouts.p: wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) x wavelength (m), v = f x λ

core.h: The two equations for wave speed
core.p: There are two ways to get wave speed. You can time a wave over a measured distance, or you can measure frequency and wavelength. Good practical answers often use both and compare them.
bullets: **v = distance / time**: time one wavefront (or pulse) travelling a measured distance.
**v = f x λ**: measure frequency and wavelength separately and multiply.
Rearranged: f = v / λ and λ = v / f.
Always convert units first: cm to m (divide by 100), mm to m (divide by 1000), kHz to Hz (multiply by 1000).
If the two methods give similar values, the result is more **reliable** (repeatable and reproducible).

core.p: A ripple tank is a shallow tray of water with a lamp above and a white screen below. The lamp shines through the water: crests act like converging lenses and make bright lines on the screen, so you can see and measure the wavefronts.
bullets: A **motor-driven dipper (vibrating bar)** dips into the water and makes straight **plane waves**.
A **signal generator / power supply** controls the frequency of the dipper.
A **lamp** above the tank projects the wave pattern onto a **white screen or paper** below.
Keep the water **shallow and of even depth**: wave speed in water depends on depth.
A **metre ruler** placed on the screen lets you measure the shadow pattern.
Darken the room so the bright lines show up clearly.

callouts.p: The pattern on the screen is larger than the real waves. Measure a known length (e.g. a ruler in the water) on the screen to find the scale, or place the ruler on the screen and only compare relative values.

core.p: Frequency is how many waves are made each second, which equals how many times the dipper vibrates each second.
bullets: Count the number of waves passing a fixed point on the screen in **10 seconds**, then divide by 10.
Counting over a longer time reduces the effect of **reaction time** error.
Or read the frequency directly from the **signal generator** setting.
Or use a **stroboscope**: increase its flash rate until the waves appear to freeze; the strobe frequency then equals the wave frequency.
A phone video with a timer can be slowed down to count waves accurately.

callouts.p: Say: count the number of waves passing a point in a measured time, then frequency = number of waves / time.

core.p: One wavelength is too small to measure accurately with a ruler, so measure across several waves and divide.
bullets: Measure the distance across, for example, **10 bright lines (10 wavelengths)** with a metre ruler.
Wavelength = total distance / number of wavelengths.
Measuring over many waves reduces the **percentage uncertainty**.
Use a **stroboscope** or take a **photograph** so the pattern is still while you measure.
Make sure you count gaps between lines (wavelengths), not the lines themselves: 11 lines make 10 wavelengths.

callouts.p: If you count 5 bright lines, there are only 4 wavelengths between them.

core.p: You can also find the speed by timing how long one wavefront takes to travel a known distance across the tank.
bullets: Mark two points a measured distance apart on the screen (e.g. 30 cm).
Time how long a single wavefront takes to travel between them.
Speed = distance / time.
Repeat several times and calculate a **mean**, ignoring **anomalous** results.
Compare with f x λ from the same set-up to check your results.
Water waves are slow (around 0.1 to 0.3 m/s), so a stopwatch is suitable.

core.h: Waves on a stretched string: set-up
core.p: A string is fixed at one end to a vibration generator and passes over a pulley with masses hanging from it to keep it under tension. A signal generator drives the vibration generator.
bullets: The **signal generator** sets the frequency; read f directly from its display.
The **vibration generator** shakes the string up and down: a **transverse** wave.
The **hanging masses** provide constant tension.
Adjust the frequency until a clear, still pattern of loops appears: a **standing (stationary) wave**.
Points that do not move are **nodes**; points with the biggest vibration are **antinodes**.
Each loop is **half a wavelength**, so two loops = one wavelength.

callouts.p: Measure the length of several whole loops with a metre ruler, divide by the number of loops to get half a wavelength, then double it.

core.h: Waves on a string: method and results
core.p: Once the frequency and wavelength are known, the speed of the wave on the string is found from v = f x λ.
bullets: Set the frequency, adjust until a clear standing wave forms, and read f from the signal generator.
Measure the length of as many whole loops as possible with a **metre ruler**.
λ = 2 x (length of the loops / number of loops).
Calculate v = f x λ.
Change the frequency to get a different number of loops; the wave speed should stay **about the same** because it depends on the string and its tension, not on the frequency.
Higher frequency gives more loops and a shorter wavelength, since λ = v / f.

callouts.p: Wave speed depends on the medium (here the string and its tension). Changing the frequency only changes the wavelength.

core.h: Speed of sound in air: echo method
core.p: Sound travels about 340 m/s in air, which is too fast to time over a short distance, so you need a long distance or electronic timing.
bullets: Stand a measured distance (e.g. **50 m or more**) from a large flat wall, measured with a **trundle wheel** or long tape measure.
Clap or bang two blocks together and time how long until the **echo** returns.
The sound travels **to the wall and back**, so the distance is **2 x d**.
Better: clap in rhythm with the echoes, time **20 claps**, and divide to get the time for one round trip.
Speed = 2d / t.

callouts.p: For an echo, the sound goes there and back. Forgetting to double the distance halves your answer.

core.h: Speed of sound: two microphones and oscilloscope
core.p: Electronic timing removes human reaction time, so it allows a much shorter distance and gives more accurate results.
bullets: Place two **microphones** a measured distance apart in line with a sound source.
Connect them to an **oscilloscope** or **data logger** (or a timer that starts and stops on each sound).
Make a sharp sound; measure the **time delay** between the two signals.
Speed = distance between microphones / time delay.
Alternative: use a signal generator and loudspeaker; move one microphone until the two traces are **in step** again; the distance moved is one wavelength, then v = f x λ.

core.h: Speed of sound in a solid
core.p: Sound travels faster in solids than in air because the particles are closer together and strongly bonded, so vibrations pass on quickly.
bullets: Hang a metal rod and tap one end with a hammer so it rings.
Use a **microphone** with an oscilloscope, or a frequency app, to find the **frequency** of the note.
For a rod tapped at the end, the length of the rod is **half a wavelength**, so λ = 2 x length.
Calculate v = f x λ.
Typical speeds are thousands of m/s, much faster than in air.

core.p: Examiners reward specific, named sources of error and specific improvements, not vague answers like human error.
bullets: **Random error**: reaction time when starting and stopping a stopwatch; reduce by timing many waves or many echoes and repeating to find a mean.
**Systematic error**: magnified shadows in a ripple tank, or a ruler with a zero error.
Measure over **many wavelengths** or a **long distance** to reduce percentage uncertainty.
Use a **stroboscope**, photo or video to freeze moving patterns.
Safety: keep water away from mains electrics; hanging masses can fall, so keep feet clear; do not overload the vibration generator.
A **resolution** of 1 mm on a ruler is fine for loops on a string but limits a single ripple wavelength.

callouts.p: Name the measurement, say how to improve it, and say why it helps, e.g. time 10 waves not 1 to reduce the effect of reaction time.

analogy.p: Imagine a band marching past you. The number of rows passing you each second is the frequency, the gap between rows is the wavelength, and how fast the band moves forward is the speed. Speed = rows per second x gap between rows, exactly like v = f x λ. It breaks down because the band members actually move along with the band, whereas in a wave the particles only vibrate about a fixed position and it is the energy that travels.

exam.q: State the equation linking wave speed, frequency and wavelength.
model: wave speed = frequency x wavelength (v = f x λ)
exam.tip: Write it in words or symbols, both are accepted.

exam.q: A student counts 24 waves passing a point in a ripple tank in 10 s. Calculate the frequency.
model: f = 2.4 Hz
exam.tip: Frequency = number of waves / time.

exam.q: Describe how to measure the wavelength of water waves in a ripple tank.
model: Measure the distance across a number of waves (e.g. 10) on the screen with a ruler
Divide by the number of wavelengths
exam.tip: Mention measuring several waves, not just one.

exam.q: Explain why the student should measure across 10 waves rather than 1.
model: One wavelength is small so the reading has a large percentage uncertainty
Measuring 10 and dividing reduces the uncertainty, giving a more accurate value
exam.tip: Use the words uncertainty or accuracy.

exam.q: The waves in a ripple tank have frequency 4.0 Hz and wavelength 3.0 cm. Calculate the wave speed in m/s.
exam.tip: Convert cm to m first.

exam.q: A student stands 85 m from a wall and hears an echo 0.50 s after clapping. Calculate the speed of sound.
model: Total distance = 2 x 85 = 170 m
exam.tip: Double the distance for an echo.

exam.q: Suggest one reason why the echo method gives an inaccurate value for the speed of sound, and an improvement.
model: Reaction time is large compared with the short time measured
Time many echoes (e.g. 20 claps) and divide, or use a longer distance, or electronic timing with microphones
exam.tip: Pair the error with a matching improvement.

exam.q: On a stretched string there are 4 loops along 1.20 m. The signal generator reads 50 Hz. Calculate the wave speed.
model: Each loop = 0.30 m so λ = 0.60 m
v = 30 m/s
exam.tip: Two loops make one wavelength.

exam.q: The frequency of the vibration generator is doubled. State and explain what happens to the wavelength on the string.
model: Wavelength halves
Wave speed is unchanged because the string and tension are the same, and λ = v / f
exam.tip: Speed depends on the medium.

exam.q: Describe how a stroboscope can be used to measure the frequency of water waves.
model: Increase the strobe frequency until the waves appear stationary
The strobe frequency then equals the wave frequency
exam.tip: Start low and increase so you find the true value.

exam.q: Describe a method to measure the speed of water waves in a ripple tank. Include how you would make your results accurate.
model: Set up a ripple tank with shallow water of even depth, lamp above and white screen below
Use a motor-driven dipper to make plane waves
Count waves passing a point in 10 s and divide by 10 to get frequency, or read signal generator
Measure the length of 10 wavelengths on the screen with a ruler and divide by 10
Calculate speed using v = f x λ
Use a stroboscope or photo to freeze the pattern; repeat and take a mean; check with distance / time for one wavefront
exam.tip: 6 mark answers need a logical sequence: set-up, measurements, calculation, accuracy.

exam.q: Describe how to measure the speed of sound in air using two microphones.
model: Place two microphones a measured distance apart (metre ruler or tape) in line with the source
Connect to an oscilloscope or electronic timer
Make a sharp sound and record the time delay between the two signals
Speed = distance / time delay; repeat and take a mean
exam.tip: Electronic timing avoids reaction time.

worked.q: In a ripple tank, 11 bright lines cover 25 cm on the screen. A student counts 30 waves in 10 s. Calculate the wave speed.
A student claps in time with the echoes from a wall 60 m away. 20 claps take 7.0 s. Calculate the speed of sound.
steps: Time for one round trip = 7.0 / 20 = 0.35 s.
Distance for one round trip = 2 x 60 = 120 m.
worked.ans: v = 343 m/s (about 340 m/s)

phy_ocra.10.4.summary: PAG P5 is the energy practical: you **determine the specific heat capacity** of a material, usually a metal block or water, by heating it electrically and measuring how much energy goes in and how much its temperature rises. You use **E = V x I x t** (or a joulemeter) for the energy supplied and **change in internal energy = mass x specific heat capacity x change in temperature** to find c. Examiners test the method, the calculation, why the measured value is usually too high, and how insulation and good thermal contact improve accuracy.

core.p: Different materials need different amounts of energy to warm up. Specific heat capacity tells you how much energy it takes to warm 1 kg of a material by 1 degree. Water has a very high value, which is why it takes a long time to boil a kettle.
bullets: Symbol **c**, unit **J/kg °C** (joules per kilogram per degree Celsius).
A **high** c means the material needs lots of energy to heat up and cools down slowly.
A **low** c means it heats up quickly with little energy, like metals.
Water: about **4200 J/kg °C**. Aluminium: about **900 J/kg °C**. Copper: about **390 J/kg °C**.
Heating a material increases the energy in its **thermal energy store** (its internal energy).

callouts.p: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C.

core.p: Two equations are combined in this practical: one for the energy put in by the electric heater and one for the energy stored by the block.
bullets: **change in internal energy = mass x specific heat capacity x change in temperature**: ΔE = m x c x Δθ.
Rearranged: **c = ΔE / (m x Δθ)**.
Energy from the heater: **energy = power x time**, E = P x t.
Electrical power: **P = V x I**, so **E = V x I x t**.
Time must be in **seconds**, mass in **kilograms**, energy in **joules**.
Δθ = final temperature minus starting temperature.

callouts.p: Assuming all the heater energy goes into the block: V x I x t = m x c x Δθ, so c = V I t / (m Δθ).

core.p: A standard 1 kg aluminium block has two holes: one for an immersion heater and one for a thermometer. The block is wrapped in insulation so that as little energy as possible escapes to the surroundings.
bullets: **Metal block** (e.g. 1 kg aluminium) with two drilled holes.
**Immersion heater** (often 12 V, about 50 W) in one hole.
**Thermometer** or temperature probe in the other hole.
A **few drops of water or oil** in the thermometer hole for good **thermal contact**.
**Insulation** (e.g. bubble wrap or foam) around the block, and a heat-proof mat underneath.
Low-voltage **power supply**, **ammeter**, **voltmeter** (or a **joulemeter**), stopwatch and top-pan balance.

core.p: Follow a clear sequence so you can write it in a 6 mark answer.
bullets: Measure the **mass** of the block with a top-pan balance and convert to kg.
Put the heater and thermometer in the holes; add a few drops of oil or water to the thermometer hole.
Wrap the block in **insulation** and stand it on a heat-proof mat.
Connect the heater to the power supply with an **ammeter in series** and a **voltmeter in parallel** (or through a joulemeter).
Record the **starting temperature**.
Switch on and start the stopwatch. Record **V** and **I** (they should stay roughly constant).
Record the temperature every **minute** for about **10 minutes**.
Switch off, but keep watching: the temperature may keep rising for a short while; record the **highest** temperature.
Calculate E = V x I x t, Δθ, and c = E / (m x Δθ).

callouts.p: If a joulemeter is used, take its reading at the start and end: energy supplied = final reading minus initial reading.

core.p: The energy supplied is found from the power of the heater and the time it is on. The ammeter and voltmeter readings give the power.
bullets: The **ammeter** goes **in series** with the heater so the same current flows through both.
The **voltmeter** goes **in parallel** (across) the heater to measure the potential difference across it.
Power P = V x I, in watts (joules per second).
Energy E = V x I x t, with t in seconds.
Use a **low-voltage** supply for safety.

callouts.p: 10 minutes is 600 s. Using 10 in E = V I t gives an answer 60 times too small.

core.h: Calculating c from a single reading
core.p: The simplest method uses the total energy supplied and the total temperature rise.
bullets: Energy supplied: E = V x I x t (or joulemeter difference).
Temperature rise: Δθ = highest temperature minus starting temperature.
c = E / (m x Δθ).
Give the answer with the unit J/kg °C and a sensible number of significant figures.
Compare with the accepted value (e.g. 900 J/kg °C for aluminium).

core.p: Plotting temperature against time uses all your readings and avoids the slow start while the heater warms up.
bullets: Plot **temperature (y-axis)** against **time (x-axis)**.
The graph curves at first (the heater and thermometer take time to warm up), then becomes a **straight line**.
Find the **gradient** of the straight part: gradient = Δθ / Δt in °C/s.
Since P x t = m x c x Δθ, rearranging gives **c = P / (m x gradient)**.
Alternatively plot **temperature against energy supplied**: then gradient = 1 / (m x c), so c = 1 / (m x gradient).
Using a straight-line section reduces the effect of the start-up delay.

callouts.p: Steeper graph = faster temperature rise = smaller specific heat capacity for the same power and mass.

core.h: Why the measured value is usually too high
core.p: In real experiments some of the energy from the heater does not stay in the block. That means the temperature rise is smaller than it should be, so the calculated c comes out bigger than the true value.
bullets: Energy is transferred to the **surroundings** by heating the air (conduction, convection) and by radiation.
Some energy warms the **heater itself**, the thermometer and the insulation.
A smaller Δθ in c = E / (m Δθ) gives a **larger c**.
So heat losses cause the measured specific heat capacity to be an **overestimate**.
Losses get worse as the block gets hotter, because the temperature difference with the room is bigger.

callouts.p: Energy lost to the surroundings makes c too HIGH, not too low. Explain using the equation: smaller Δθ for the same E.

core.p: Each improvement should target a specific source of error.
bullets: **Insulate** the block (and put a lid of insulation on top) to reduce energy transfer to the surroundings.
Put **oil or water** in the thermometer hole to improve **thermal contact**, so the thermometer reads the block temperature.
Use a **digital temperature probe and data logger** for better resolution and no reading errors.
Record the **maximum** temperature after switching off, because heat still flows from the hot heater into the block.
Keep the temperature rise **moderate** (e.g. about 10 °C) so losses stay small but Δθ is still large enough to measure accurately.
Use the **graph method** rather than a single pair of readings.
Repeat and compare with the accepted value.

callouts.p: Answers like 'insulate the block to reduce thermal energy transfer to the surroundings' score; 'make it a fair test' does not.

core.h: Using water instead of a metal block
core.p: The same method works for water in an insulated beaker or polystyrene cup.
bullets: Measure the mass of water using a balance (or 1 cm³ of water has a mass of about 1 g).
Put the immersion heater and thermometer in the water.
**Stir** the water so the temperature is even throughout.
Use a polystyrene cup or lagged beaker with a lid to reduce losses, including **evaporation**.
Expected value: about 4200 J/kg °C.

core.p: Knowing which variable is which helps with planning questions.
bullets: **Independent variable**: the material being tested (or time / energy supplied for the graph).
**Dependent variable**: the temperature rise.
**Control variables**: mass of block, power of heater, starting temperature, amount of insulation.
Safety: the heater and block get **hot**, so do not touch them and let them cool before handling.
Do not switch the heater on unless it is in the block or in water, or it may overheat.
Keep water away from electrical connections.

core.p: This practical shows conservation of energy: the energy is transferred electrically from the supply to the heater, then by heating to the block.
bullets: Energy transferred **electrically** by the current does work in the heater.
The heater transfers energy **by heating** to the **thermal energy store** of the block.
Energy is never destroyed: the energy 'lost' is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings and is **dissipated**.
Efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input; here, useful energy = m x c x Δθ for the block.

callouts.p: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred usefully, stored or dissipated.

analogy.p: Think of temperature as the water level and energy as water poured in from a tap (the heater). A material with a high specific heat capacity is like a very wide bucket: you pour in a lot of water but the level rises only a little. A low specific heat capacity is a narrow bucket where the level shoots up. Heat losses are like a leak in the bucket: the level rises less than it should, so you would wrongly think the bucket is wider (c too high). It breaks down because buckets have a fixed size, while real materials also lose energy faster as they get hotter.

terms.d: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C, in J/kg °C.
The total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles in a system.
The energy store that increases when an object is heated and its temperature rises.
A measure of how hot an object is, linked to the average kinetic energy of its particles, in °C.
The rate of energy transfer, in watts; 1 W = 1 J/s.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points, in volts; measured with a voltmeter in parallel.
The rate of flow of charge, in amperes; measured with an ammeter in series.
A meter that measures the electrical energy supplied to a device directly, in joules.
An electric heater designed to be placed inside a liquid or a hole in a block to heat it.
How well heat can pass between two objects; improved by filling air gaps with oil or water.
Material that reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating to the surroundings.
Energy spread out to the surroundings, usually in thermal stores, so it is no longer useful.
The slope of a graph: change in y divided by change in x.
An error that shifts every result in the same direction, such as heat loss making c too high.
The smallest change in a quantity that an instrument can detect.

mistakes.w: Heat losses make the specific heat capacity too low.
mistakes.r: Heat losses make Δθ smaller for the same energy, so c = E / (m Δθ) is too high.

mistakes.w: Using time in minutes in E = V x I x t.
mistakes.r: Convert time to seconds before calculating energy.

mistakes.w: Using mass in grams in ΔE = m c Δθ.
mistakes.r: Convert grams to kilograms (divide by 1000).

mistakes.w: Using the final temperature as Δθ.
mistakes.r: Δθ is final temperature minus starting temperature.

mistakes.w: Putting the voltmeter in series with the heater.
mistakes.r: The voltmeter goes in parallel across the heater; the ammeter goes in series.

mistakes.w: Insulation makes the block heat up faster because it traps the heat.
mistakes.r: Insulation reduces energy transfer to the surroundings, so more of the energy supplied stays in the block.

mistakes.w: Repeat the experiment to make it more accurate.
mistakes.r: Repeating and taking a mean reduces random error; to improve accuracy reduce heat losses (insulation, lid) and improve thermal contact.

mistakes.w: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to heat a substance.
mistakes.r: It is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of the substance by 1 °C.

exam.q: Define specific heat capacity.
model: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C
exam.tip: Include both 1 kg and 1 °C.

exam.q: State the equation linking change in internal energy, mass, specific heat capacity and change in temperature.
model: change in internal energy = mass x specific heat capacity x change in temperature
exam.tip: ΔE = m c Δθ.

exam.q: A heater with p.d. 12 V and current 4.0 A is switched on for 5 minutes. Calculate the energy supplied.
exam.tip: Convert minutes to seconds.

exam.q: A 1.0 kg block receives 14 400 J and its temperature rises by 16 °C. Calculate its specific heat capacity.
model: c = ΔE / (m Δθ)
c = 900 J/kg °C
exam.tip: Rearrange before substituting.

exam.q: Explain why a few drops of oil are put in the thermometer hole.
model: Oil fills the air gap and improves thermal contact
So the thermometer reads the true temperature of the block
exam.tip: Air is a poor conductor.

exam.q: The student's value for c is higher than the accepted value. Explain why.
model: Some energy is transferred to the surroundings (or heats the heater and thermometer)
So the temperature rise is smaller than it would be
c = E / (m Δθ) so a smaller Δθ gives a larger c
exam.tip: Link the error to the equation.

exam.q: Suggest two improvements to reduce the error in this experiment.
model: Wrap the block in (more) insulation and put a lid on top
Use a temperature probe and data logger / record the maximum temperature after switching off / use a graph of the straight section
exam.tip: Each improvement should match a source of error.

exam.q: Explain why the temperature of the block may continue to rise after the heater is switched off.
model: The heater is hotter than the block
Energy continues to transfer by heating from the heater to the block
exam.tip: Record the highest temperature reached.

exam.q: The straight part of a temperature-time graph has a gradient of 0.050 °C/s. The heater power is 45 W and the mass is 1.0 kg. Calculate c.
model: P = m x c x gradient
c = 900 J/kg °C
exam.tip: Power = energy per second, so P = m c (Δθ / Δt).

exam.q: Describe how to determine the specific heat capacity of a metal block. Include how to process the results.
model: Measure the mass of the block with a balance
Place immersion heater and thermometer in holes, oil in thermometer hole, insulate block
Connect heater to supply with ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel (or use a joulemeter)
Record start temperature, switch on and record temperature every minute for about 10 minutes, and record V and I
Energy = V x I x t and Δθ = final minus initial temperature
c = E / (m x Δθ), or plot temperature against time and use c = P / (m x gradient)
exam.tip: Give a logical order and name every instrument.

worked.q: A 0.80 kg copper block is heated by a 30 W heater for 4.0 minutes. Its temperature rises from 20 °C to 43 °C. Calculate the specific heat capacity of copper from these results.
worked.ans: c = 391 J/kg °C (about 390 J/kg °C)

worked.q: A joulemeter reads 12 500 J at the start and 33 500 J at the end. 0.50 kg of water rises from 18 °C to 28 °C. Calculate c and suggest why it differs from 4200 J/kg °C.

worked.ans: c = 4200 J/kg °C, matching the accepted value; real results are usually slightly higher because of heat losses.

worked.ans: 27 000 J, taking 540 s (9 minutes)

phy_ocra.10.5.summary: PAG P6 is about measuring how the **current through a component changes with the potential difference across it**, and how the resistance of sensing components changes with conditions. You build a circuit with an **ammeter in series**, a **voltmeter in parallel** and a **variable resistor** (or variable supply), then plot **I-V characteristics** for a fixed resistor, a filament lamp and a diode, and investigate how a **thermistor** and an **LDR** respond to temperature and light. Examiners test the circuit, the shapes of the graphs, explanations of the shapes using R = V / I, and how to make the results accurate and safe.

core.p: Every circuit component practical comes back to three quantities: current, potential difference and resistance. Resistance tells you how hard it is for current to flow through a component.
bullets: **Current (I)**: rate of flow of charge, in amperes (A).
**Potential difference (V)**: energy transferred per unit charge, in volts (V).
**Resistance (R)**: in ohms (Ω).
**V = I x R**, so **R = V / I**.
For a given p.d., a **bigger resistance** gives a **smaller current**.
Resistance at any point on an I-V graph = V / I at that point (not the gradient).

callouts.p: potential difference (V) = current (A) x resistance (Ω), V = I x R

core.h: The circuit for an I-V characteristic
core.p: To find how current varies with p.d. you need to measure both while changing the p.d. across the component in steps.
bullets: **Ammeter in series** with the component, so the same current passes through both.
**Voltmeter in parallel** across the component, to measure the p.d. across it only.
A **variable resistor** (rheostat) in series, or a **variable power supply**, to change the p.d. in steps.
Reverse the connections to the component (or the supply) to get **negative** values of V and I.
A **switch** lets you turn the current off between readings.

callouts.p: An ammeter in parallel or a voltmeter in series is the most common circuit mistake. Ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel.

core.p: A clear method lets you score full marks on the 6 mark planning question.
bullets: Set up the circuit with the component, ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel and a variable resistor.
Adjust the variable resistor to give a small p.d.; record **V** and **I**.
Change the p.d. in **equal steps** (e.g. 0.5 V) and record at least **6 to 8** pairs of readings.
**Reverse** the component (or the supply) and repeat to get negative values.
**Repeat** each reading and calculate a mean.
Plot **current (y-axis)** against **potential difference (x-axis)** and draw a line or curve of best fit through the origin.
Switch off between readings so the component does not heat up unnecessarily.

callouts.p: OCR I-V graphs usually have current on the y-axis and p.d. on the x-axis. Read the axes before describing the gradient.

core.p: For a resistor (or a wire) kept at a constant temperature, current is directly proportional to potential difference.
bullets: The I-V graph is a **straight line through the origin**.
Reversing the p.d. gives the same shape in the negative quadrant.
Resistance is **constant**: R = V / I is the same at every point.
This is **Ohm's law**: current is directly proportional to p.d. at constant temperature.
A steeper line (I against V) means a **smaller** resistance.

callouts.p: For a conductor at constant temperature, the current through it is directly proportional to the potential difference across it.

core.p: A filament lamp is a thin metal wire that gets very hot. As the current increases, the filament heats up and its resistance increases.
bullets: The I-V graph is a **curve**: steep near the origin and **flattening** at higher p.d.
Same shape for negative p.d. (it is symmetrical through the origin).
As current increases, the filament **temperature rises**.
Metal ions **vibrate more**, so electrons **collide** with them more often.
This makes it harder for charge to flow, so **resistance increases**.
Equal increases in p.d. give **smaller and smaller increases** in current.

callouts.p: Current up, temperature up, ions vibrate more, more collisions, resistance up, graph curves.

core.p: A diode lets current flow in one direction only. It is used to protect circuits and to convert alternating current to direct current.
bullets: In the **reverse** direction the resistance is **very high**, so the current is **zero** (or almost zero).
In the **forward** direction no current flows until the p.d. reaches about **0.6 V** (for a silicon diode).
Above this the current **rises steeply**: resistance becomes **low**.
A **light-emitting diode (LED)** behaves in the same way and gives out light when current flows forwards.
Use a **protective resistor** in series so the current does not get too large and damage the diode.
