core.p: A thermistor is a temperature-dependent resistor. Its resistance changes a lot as its temperature changes, which makes it useful as a temperature sensor.
bullets: For the common (NTC) thermistor: as **temperature increases**, **resistance decreases**.
The graph of resistance against temperature is a **curve** that falls steeply then levels off.
Investigate it by placing the thermistor in a **beaker of water** heated in steps (or with ice and hot water), with a **thermometer** in the water.
At each temperature measure V and I and calculate **R = V / I**, or use an **ohmmeter** (multimeter).
Stir the water and wait for the reading to settle so the thermistor is at the water temperature.
Uses: thermostats, fire alarms, car engine temperature sensors.

callouts.p: Seal the thermistor legs (e.g. in a test tube or with a waterproof covering) so the water does not short-circuit the leads.

core.p: An LDR is a resistor whose resistance depends on the light falling on it.
bullets: As **light intensity increases**, **resistance decreases**.
In the dark its resistance is very high; in bright light it is low.
Investigate by shining a lamp on it from different **distances** (closer = brighter), or use a **light meter** to measure intensity.
Measure R with an ohmmeter, or with an ammeter and voltmeter and R = V / I.
Do it in a **darkened room** so only the lamp affects the LDR.
Uses: automatic street lights, night lights, light-sensitive alarms.

core.p: You often have to calculate resistance from a pair of readings or from a point on a graph.
bullets: Resistance at a point: **R = V / I** using the readings at that point.
For a straight line through the origin, R is the same everywhere.
For a curve, R is **different** at each point; calculate it separately for each reading.
Convert milliamps to amps: divide by 1000 (e.g. 25 mA = 0.025 A).
Do not use the gradient of a curve to find resistance; use V / I at the point.

callouts.p: If the current is in mA, convert before using R = V / I or your answer will be 1000 times too small.

core.p: Name variables and errors precisely to pick up method marks.
bullets: I-V practical: **independent** = p.d., **dependent** = current, **control** = the component, its temperature (for a resistor), the type of meter.
Thermistor practical: independent = temperature; dependent = resistance.
LDR practical: independent = light intensity (or distance of lamp); dependent = resistance.
**Heating effect**: current heats the resistor and changes its resistance; switch off between readings and use small currents.
**Zero error**: check meters read zero when no current flows.
Use meters with suitable **resolution** (e.g. a milliammeter for small currents).
Take **repeat readings** and calculate means to reduce random error.

core.p: These practicals use low voltages, but components and wires can still get hot.
bullets: Use a **low-voltage** supply.
Do not touch the filament lamp or resistors when hot.
Use a **protective resistor** with a diode or LED.
Switch off between readings to avoid overheating.
Keep water well away from the power supply in the thermistor investigation; use an electric kettle or water bath safely.

core.p: Examiners often ask how a sensing component can be used in a real circuit.
bullets: Thermistor or LDR in a **potential divider** gives an output p.d. that changes with temperature or light.
Street lamp: LDR resistance rises when it gets dark, which changes the p.d. across it and switches on the lamp.
Fire alarm or thermostat: thermistor resistance falls as it gets hot, changing the current or p.d.
Diodes protect circuits from current flowing the wrong way (e.g. if a battery is put in backwards).

analogy.p: Picture electrons as students walking down a corridor and the metal ions as people standing in it. In a cool resistor the people stand still, so the flow is steady and the same push always gives the same flow (a straight line). In a hot filament the people jostle about, so students bump into them more and the flow is harder (resistance rises). A diode is a one-way turnstile that only opens once you push hard enough in the right direction. The analogy breaks down because electrons are pushed by the p.d. all at once around the whole circuit, not one by one, and they drift very slowly.

terms.d: The rate of flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (A).
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points in a circuit, measured in volts (V).
The opposition to current flow; R = V / I, measured in ohms (Ω).
A graph showing how the current through a component varies with the potential difference across it.
A conductor where current is directly proportional to potential difference at constant temperature.
At constant temperature, current through a conductor is directly proportional to the p.d. across it.
A lamp with a thin metal wire whose resistance increases as its temperature increases.
A component that allows current to flow in one direction only; very high resistance in reverse.
A diode that emits light when current flows through it in the forward direction.
A resistor whose resistance decreases as its temperature increases.
A resistor whose resistance decreases as the light intensity on it increases.
Meter that measures current; connected in series with the component.
Meter that measures potential difference; connected in parallel across the component.
A resistor whose resistance can be changed, used to change the current and p.d. in a circuit.
A meter (often part of a multimeter) that measures resistance directly.
Two resistors in series that share the supply p.d.; used with sensors to give a changing output p.d.

mistakes.w: The resistance of a filament lamp increases because the wire gets longer.
mistakes.r: Temperature rises, ions vibrate more, electrons collide with them more often, so resistance increases.

mistakes.w: The voltmeter is connected in series.
mistakes.r: The voltmeter is connected in parallel across the component; the ammeter is in series.

mistakes.w: A diode lets no current through at all.
mistakes.r: A diode lets current through in the forward direction only (above about 0.6 V); reverse current is zero.

mistakes.w: A thermistor's resistance increases when it gets hotter.
mistakes.r: Thermistor resistance decreases as temperature increases.

mistakes.w: LDR resistance increases with more light.
mistakes.r: LDR resistance decreases as light intensity increases.

mistakes.w: Resistance is the gradient of the I-V graph.
mistakes.r: Resistance = V / I at a given point; for current on the y-axis the gradient is 1 / R only for a straight line.

mistakes.w: The graph for a resistor is a straight line.
mistakes.r: A straight line through the origin, showing current is directly proportional to p.d.

mistakes.w: Using 25 mA as 25 A in R = V / I.
mistakes.r: Convert mA to A by dividing by 1000 first.

exam.q: State the equation linking potential difference, current and resistance.
model: potential difference = current x resistance (V = I x R)
exam.tip: Learn it in words and symbols.

exam.q: Draw or describe where the ammeter and voltmeter must be placed to measure the I-V characteristic of a lamp.
model: Ammeter in series with the lamp
Voltmeter in parallel across the lamp
exam.tip: Draw circuit symbols correctly, with no gaps in wires.

exam.q: A resistor has a p.d. of 6.0 V across it and a current of 0.30 A. Calculate its resistance.
model: R = 20 Ω
exam.tip: Rearrange V = I R.

exam.q: The current through a component is 40 mA when the p.d. is 2.0 V. Calculate its resistance.
model: R = 50 Ω
exam.tip: Convert mA to A.

exam.q: Describe the I-V graph for a fixed resistor at constant temperature.
model: Straight line
Through the origin (current directly proportional to p.d.)
exam.tip: Both features are needed.

exam.q: Explain the shape of the I-V graph for a filament lamp.
model: Graph is a curve whose gradient decreases at higher p.d.
As current increases the filament temperature increases
Ions in the metal vibrate more so electrons collide more often
So resistance increases
exam.tip: Give the full chain from current to resistance.

exam.q: Describe the I-V characteristic of a diode.
model: No current in the reverse direction (very high resistance)
No current in forward direction until about 0.6 V
Then current increases rapidly (low resistance)
exam.tip: Mention both directions.

exam.q: Describe how the resistance of a thermistor changes as temperature increases.
model: Resistance decreases
exam.tip: Thermistor: hotter means lower resistance.

exam.q: Suggest why the variable resistor is needed in the I-V circuit.
model: To change the current (and p.d.) through the component so several readings can be taken
exam.tip: It controls the independent variable.

exam.q: Explain why the student should switch off the circuit between readings when testing a fixed resistor.
model: Current heats the resistor
This would change its resistance, so the temperature would not be constant
exam.tip: Ohm's law needs constant temperature.

exam.q: Describe how to investigate how the resistance of a thermistor varies with temperature.
model: Connect the thermistor to an ohmmeter, or to a supply with an ammeter in series and voltmeter in parallel
Place the thermistor (waterproofed) in a beaker of water with a thermometer
Heat the water / add hot water to change the temperature in steps, e.g. every 10 °C
Stir and wait for readings to stabilise, then record temperature and resistance (or V and I)
Calculate R = V / I for each temperature
Repeat, find means, and plot resistance against temperature
exam.tip: Include how temperature is changed and measured as well as how resistance is found.

worked.q: A student's readings for a filament lamp are 1.0 V, 0.20 A and 4.0 V, 0.40 A. Calculate the resistance at each p.d. and explain the difference.
steps: Higher current makes the filament hotter.
Ions vibrate more, electrons collide more, so resistance increases.
worked.ans: 5.0 Ω at 1.0 V and 10 Ω at 4.0 V; the resistance increases because the filament gets hotter.

worked.q: A diode is connected to 3.0 V with a 100 Ω protective resistor in series. The p.d. across the diode is 0.7 V. Calculate the current.
steps: P.d. across resistor = 3.0 - 0.7 = 2.3 V (p.d.s add up in series).

worked.q: A thermistor has a p.d. of 5.0 V and a current of 2.5 mA at 20 °C, and a current of 10 mA at 60 °C with the same p.d. Find the resistance at each temperature.
worked.ans: 2000 Ω at 20 °C and 500 Ω at 60 °C: resistance falls as temperature rises.

phy_ocra.10.6.summary: PAG P7 is the practical where you **build series and parallel circuits** and use ammeters and voltmeters to find the rules for **current, potential difference and resistance** in each. In a **series** circuit the current is the same everywhere and the p.d. is shared, so resistances add up. In a **parallel** circuit each branch gets the full p.d. and the currents in the branches add up to the total, so adding resistors in parallel **reduces** the total resistance. Examiners test the circuit diagrams, the measurements, the rules and the reasoning behind them.

core.p: Real circuits, from torches to house wiring, are built from components connected in series, in parallel or a mixture. This practical lets you discover the rules by measuring current and potential difference at different places in each type of circuit.
bullets: **Series**: components connected one after another in a single loop.
**Parallel**: components connected on separate branches, each joined directly across the supply.
Measure **current** with an **ammeter in series** at different points.
Measure **p.d.** with a **voltmeter in parallel** across each component and across the supply.
Calculate resistance using **R = V / I**.
Compare the total resistance of resistors in series and in parallel.

callouts.p: potential difference = current x resistance, V = I x R

core.p: In a series circuit there is only one path, so every charge must pass through every component. Charge is not used up, so the rate of flow is the same everywhere.
bullets: The **current is the same at every point** in a series circuit.
Ammeters placed before, between and after components all give the **same reading**.
This is because **charge is conserved**: it cannot be used up or pile up anywhere.
Adding more resistors in series **reduces** the current, because the total resistance increases.
If one component breaks, the circuit is broken and **all** components stop working.

core.h: Potential difference in a series circuit
core.p: The supply gives each coulomb of charge a certain amount of energy. In a series circuit that energy is shared between the components the charge passes through.
bullets: The **p.d. of the supply is shared** between the components.
**V total = V1 + V2 + ...**
The component with the **bigger resistance** gets the **bigger share** of the p.d. (since V = I x R and I is the same).
This is because energy is **conserved**: the energy given to each charge by the supply equals the energy it transfers in the components.
Identical components in series share the p.d. equally.

callouts.p: In series, V1 / V2 = R1 / R2. A 20 Ω and 10 Ω resistor on a 6 V supply get 4 V and 2 V.

core.p: Each resistor in series makes it harder for the charge to flow around the single loop, so their effects add together.
bullets: **R total = R1 + R2 + ...**
Adding a resistor in series **increases** the total resistance.
So the **current decreases** for the same supply p.d.
Check it experimentally: total R = supply p.d. / current, and compare with R1 + R2.
Each resistor's value can be found from R = V / I using its own voltmeter reading and the circuit current.

callouts.p: Total resistance of resistors in series is the sum of the individual resistances.

core.h: Potential difference in a parallel circuit
core.p: In a parallel circuit, each branch is connected directly across the supply, so each charge going through any one branch gets the full energy from the supply.
bullets: The **p.d. across each branch is the same** and equal to the supply p.d.
A voltmeter across any branch reads the same as one across the supply (ignoring wire resistance).
Each component works **independently**: if one branch breaks, the others still work.
This is why house lights and sockets are wired in **parallel**.

core.p: At a junction the current splits between the branches, and the branches join again before returning to the supply. Charge is conserved, so nothing is lost at the junctions.
bullets: **I total = I1 + I2 + ...**: the branch currents add up to the total current.
The current into a junction equals the current out of it.
The branch with the **smaller resistance** carries the **bigger current** (I = V / R with the same V).
Identical branches carry equal currents.
Adding another branch **increases** the total current from the supply.

callouts.p: The total current entering a junction equals the total current leaving it.

core.p: Adding a branch gives the charge an extra path to flow along. More current flows for the same p.d., so the total resistance goes down.
bullets: Adding a resistor in parallel **decreases** the total resistance.
The total resistance is **less than the smallest** individual resistance.
Reason: the p.d. across each branch stays the same, so each branch adds its own current; the **total current increases** while V is unchanged, and R = V / I falls.
Find total resistance experimentally: R total = supply p.d. / total current.
Two identical resistors in parallel have a total resistance of **half** of one of them.

core.p: This is the sequence to describe if asked how to test the series rules.
bullets: Connect a low-voltage supply, a switch and two (or more) resistors or lamps in series.
Place an ammeter at different points (e.g. before R1, between R1 and R2, after R2); record each reading.
Connect a voltmeter across the supply, then across R1, then across R2; record each reading.
Check that the currents are equal and that V1 + V2 = supply p.d.
Calculate each resistance with R = V / I, and total resistance = supply p.d. / current.
Add a third resistor and repeat to see the effect on current and total resistance.

core.p: The parallel investigation measures the current in each branch and the main line.
bullets: Connect two resistors or lamps in parallel across a low-voltage supply with a switch.
Place an ammeter in the **main line** and one in **each branch**.
Connect a voltmeter across each branch and across the supply.
Check that branch currents add up to the main current and the p.d.s are all equal.
Calculate total resistance = supply p.d. / total current and compare with each individual resistance.
Add more branches one at a time and record how the total current and resistance change.

core.p: Good technique with meters is where many practical marks are won or lost.
bullets: **Ammeter**: always in **series**; it has a very low resistance so it does not change the current.
**Voltmeter**: always in **parallel**; it has a very high resistance so almost no current flows through it.
Check meters read **zero** before switching on (no **zero error**).
Choose a suitable **range** (e.g. mA for small currents) for good **resolution**.
Connect the positive terminal of the meter towards the positive of the supply.
Switch off between readings so resistors do not heat up and change resistance.

callouts.p: Use correct symbols, a ruler, no gaps in wires, and put voltmeters on a loop that joins either side of the component.

core.p: Real results rarely match the rules exactly. Explaining why shows grade 9 understanding.
bullets: Small differences (e.g. V1 + V2 slightly less than supply p.d.) come from the **resistance of the connecting wires** and the **internal resistance** of the supply.
Meter **resolution** limits how precisely readings can be compared.
**Heating** of resistors changes their resistance during the experiment.
Repeat readings and calculate means to reduce **random errors**.
Use the **same meter** moved to different positions to avoid differences between meters (a **systematic error**).

core.p: Low-voltage circuits are safe, but sensible precautions are still expected in a method.
bullets: Use a **low-voltage** d.c. supply and do not create a short circuit (a wire straight across the supply).
Resistors and lamps can get **hot**; do not touch them while the current is on.
Switch off before changing the circuit.
**Series** uses: simple switches controlling a lamp, fuses (in series with the appliance), and sensor potential dividers.
**Parallel** uses: household lighting and ring mains, car headlights, so each device gets the full p.d. and can be switched independently.

analogy.p: Think of current as cars per minute and resistors as narrow sections of road. In series, cars must pass through one narrow section after another, so every extra narrow bit slows the whole flow and the number of cars per minute is the same everywhere along the single road. In parallel, adding a second road beside the first gives cars another route, so more cars can get through per minute and the overall hold-up is smaller. It breaks down because cars use up fuel and can park, while electric charge is never used up and never piles up anywhere in the circuit.

terms.d: A circuit in which components are connected one after another in a single loop.
A circuit in which components are connected on separate branches, each connected across the supply.
The rate of flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (A).
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points, measured in volts (V).
The opposition to the flow of current; R = V / I, measured in ohms (Ω).
A point in a circuit where the current splits into branches or branches join.
One of the separate paths in a parallel circuit.
A meter with very low resistance, connected in series, that measures current.
A meter with very high resistance, connected in parallel, that measures potential difference.
The single resistance that would have the same effect on the current as the combination of resistors.
Charge is not used up in a circuit, so current into a junction equals current out.
The energy given to charge by the supply equals the energy transferred by the components, so p.d.s in series add up.
A very low-resistance path across a supply, causing a dangerously large current.
A meter showing a non-zero reading when it should read zero, giving a systematic error.
Resistance inside the power supply or cell, which means slightly less p.d. is available to the circuit.

mistakes.w: Current gets used up as it goes round a series circuit.
mistakes.r: Current is the same at every point in a series circuit; charge is conserved and not used up.

mistakes.w: In parallel, the p.d. is shared between the branches.
mistakes.r: In parallel, each branch has the same p.d. as the supply; it is the current that splits.

mistakes.w: Adding a resistor in parallel increases the total resistance.
mistakes.r: Adding a resistor in parallel decreases the total resistance because there is an extra path for current.

mistakes.w: The voltmeter is connected in series with the resistor.
mistakes.r: The voltmeter is connected in parallel across the resistor.

mistakes.w: The biggest resistor in series has the biggest current.
mistakes.r: All series components have the same current; the biggest resistor has the biggest p.d.

mistakes.w: In parallel, the biggest resistor has the biggest current.
mistakes.r: In parallel, the smallest resistance has the biggest current, since I = V / R with the same V.

mistakes.w: The total resistance of 10 Ω and 10 Ω in parallel is 20 Ω.
mistakes.r: It is 5 Ω: less than the smallest resistor (half of one for two identical resistors).

mistakes.w: Electrons flow from positive to negative.
mistakes.r: Conventional current flows from positive to negative; electrons flow from negative to positive.

exam.q: State how the current varies around a series circuit.
model: The current is the same at every point
exam.tip: Do not say current is used up.

exam.q: Two resistors are in series with a 9.0 V battery. The p.d. across one is 6.0 V. State the p.d. across the other.
exam.tip: P.d.s in series add up to the supply p.d.

exam.q: Calculate the total resistance of a 15 Ω and a 25 Ω resistor in series.
exam.tip: Series resistances add.

exam.q: A 6.0 V supply is connected to a 10 Ω and a 20 Ω resistor in series. Calculate the current.
model: Total R = 30 Ω
exam.tip: Find total resistance first.

exam.q: For the circuit above, calculate the p.d. across the 20 Ω resistor.
exam.tip: Same current in every series component.

exam.q: In a parallel circuit, the branch currents are 0.30 A and 0.50 A. State the current from the supply.
exam.tip: Branch currents add up.

exam.q: A 12 V supply is connected across two resistors in parallel, 6.0 Ω and 4.0 Ω. Calculate the total current and the total resistance.
model: Total I = 5.0 A
exam.tip: Each branch has the full 12 V.

exam.q: Explain why adding a resistor in parallel reduces the total resistance of a circuit.
model: The new branch provides an extra path for charge to flow
The p.d. across each branch stays the same, so the total current increases
R = V / I, so with larger I and the same V the total resistance decreases
exam.tip: Link the extra path to more current.

exam.q: Give two advantages of wiring lights in a house in parallel rather than in series.
model: Each light gets the full supply p.d. so it is at full brightness
Each light can be switched on and off independently / if one fails the others stay on
exam.tip: Refer to p.d. and independence.

exam.q: A student finds that V1 + V2 is slightly less than the supply p.d. Suggest a reason.
model: Resistance of connecting wires (or internal resistance of supply, or meter resolution)
exam.tip: Name a specific cause.

exam.q: Describe how a student could investigate how the current and potential difference vary in series and parallel circuits.
model: Build a series circuit of two resistors, a low-voltage supply and switch
Move an ammeter to several points to show current is the same everywhere
Use a voltmeter across each resistor and the supply to show V1 + V2 = supply p.d.
Build a parallel circuit with ammeters in each branch and the main line
Show branch currents add up to the main current and that the p.d. across each branch equals the supply p.d.
Calculate R = V / I to compare total resistance in series and parallel; repeat readings for reliability
exam.tip: Cover both circuits, both meters and a conclusion.

worked.q: A 12 V battery is connected in series with a 30 Ω resistor and a 10 Ω resistor. Find the current and the p.d. across each resistor.
steps: I = V / R = 12 / 40 = 0.30 A (same through both).
Check: 9.0 + 3.0 = 12 V, equal to the supply.
worked.ans: 0.30 A; 9.0 V across 30 Ω and 3.0 V across 10 Ω

worked.q: Two identical 20 Ω resistors are in parallel across a 6.0 V supply. Find the total current and total resistance.
worked.ans: 0.60 A total; total resistance 10 Ω, half of one resistor and less than the smallest.

worked.q: A student measures: supply 4.5 V, main current 0.75 A, branch A current 0.45 A in a two-branch parallel circuit. Find the current in branch B and the resistance of each branch.
steps: Total R = 4.5 / 0.75 = 6.0 Ω, less than 10 Ω as expected.
worked.ans: Branch B current 0.30 A; branch A 10 Ω, branch B 15 Ω, total 6.0 Ω

phy_ocra.10.7.summary: PAG P8 Interactions of waves is the practical activity group where you investigate what happens when waves meet surfaces and materials: **reflection** from a plane mirror, **refraction** through a glass or Perspex block, **transmission and absorption** of light by coloured filters and transparent materials, and the **emission and absorption of infrared** by different surfaces. You must be able to plan the method, name the variables, draw accurate ray diagrams with normals, measure angles with a protractor, and explain the results using wave ideas.

core.p: OCR groups the required practical techniques into Practical Activity Groups (PAGs). PAG P8 is about how waves interact with matter. Questions on it can appear in any paper and often ask you to describe a method, spot errors, or analyse data.
bullets: **Reflection** of light from a plane mirror: angle of incidence = angle of reflection.
**Refraction** of light at the boundary between air and glass, Perspex or water.
**Transmission and absorption** of light by coloured filters and different transparent materials.
**Emission and absorption of infrared radiation** by different surfaces (for example using a Leslie cube).
All angles are measured **from the normal**, never from the surface.
Results must be explained using ideas of wave speed, wavelength and energy transfer.

head: Investigation
Independent variable
Dependent variable
Key control
rows: Same block and colour of light

callouts.p: Every angle in a ray experiment is measured between the ray and the **normal**, the line drawn at 90 degrees to the surface where the ray hits it.

core.p: Most of PAG P8 uses a ray box (or lamp with a slit) to make a narrow beam of light, so that its path can be traced accurately on paper.
bullets: **Ray box** with a single slit gives a narrow ray, which makes the path easy to mark.
**Protractor** to measure angles, a sharp pencil and ruler to draw rays and normals.
Plain white paper so the ray can be seen and marked with crosses.
Ray boxes get **hot**: do not touch the lamp housing and let it cool before packing away.
Work in a **dimmed room** so the ray is clearly visible, but keep the floor clear to avoid tripping.
For the infrared practical, the Leslie cube is filled with **very hot water**: handle with care to avoid scalds.

callouts.p: In a risk question give the hazard (hot ray box or hot water), the risk (burns or scalds) and the control (let it cool, do not touch the lamp, place cube on a heat-proof mat).

core.h: Reflection from a plane mirror: method
core.p: This investigation tests the **law of reflection**. You compare the angle at which a ray hits a mirror with the angle at which it leaves.
bullets: Draw a straight line on paper and stand the plane mirror upright along it.
Draw a **normal** at 90 degrees to the line using a protractor.
Shine a narrow ray from the ray box so it hits the mirror where the normal meets it.
Mark the incident and reflected rays with two crosses each, far apart, then join them with a ruler.
Measure the **angle of incidence** and **angle of reflection** from the normal.
Repeat for several angles of incidence, for example 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 degrees.

callouts.p: The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, both measured from the normal.

fig.cap: Reflection from a plane mirror. The normal is drawn at 90 degrees to the mirror, and the angle of incidence i equals the angle of reflection r.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="40" y="180" width="320" height="10" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1b2540"/><line x1="200" y1="40" x2="200" y2="180" stroke="#6b7280" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="70" y1="50" x2="200" y2="180" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="200" y1="180" x2="330" y2="50" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/><polygon points="130,110 124,98 118,104" fill="#dc2626"/><polygon points="270,110 264,110 270,104" fill="#dc2626"/><text x="186" y="150" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">i</text><text x="208" y="150" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">r</text><text x="206" y="34" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">normal</text><text x="20" y="36" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">incident ray</text><text x="300" y="36" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">reflected ray</text><text x="150" y="210" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">plane mirror</text></svg>

core.p: Results should show that the angle of reflection is always equal to the angle of incidence, within experimental error. A graph of angle of reflection against angle of incidence is a straight line through the origin with gradient 1.
bullets: Small differences (1 or 2 degrees) are due to **random error**, such as the width of the ray or reading the protractor.
A **thin ray** and crosses marked far apart reduce error in drawing the ray.
Reflection from a smooth, flat surface is **specular reflection**: parallel rays stay parallel, so a clear image forms.
Reflection from a rough surface is **diffuse reflection**: each part of the surface has a different normal, so rays scatter and no clear image forms.
The law of reflection still applies at every point on a rough surface; only the direction of the normal changes.

callouts.p: Mark the ray path with crosses at least 5 cm apart, use a sharp pencil, and read the protractor at eye level to avoid parallax.

core.h: Refraction through a rectangular block: method
core.p: Refraction is the change in direction of a wave when it crosses a boundary between two materials at an angle, because its **speed changes**.
bullets: Place a rectangular glass (or Perspex) block on paper and draw round it.
Draw a normal at the point where the ray will enter the block.
Shine a narrow ray at the block at a measured angle of incidence.
Mark the ray entering and leaving the block with crosses, remove the block and join up the path.
Measure the **angle of incidence** in air and the **angle of refraction** in the block, both from the normal.
Repeat for a range of angles of incidence and record results in a table.

callouts.p: The change in direction of a wave as it passes from one medium into another, caused by a change in the speed of the wave.

fig.cap: Refraction through a rectangular glass block. The ray bends towards the normal on entering the glass and away from the normal on leaving, so the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="120" y="80" width="170" height="90" fill="#bbf7d0" stroke="#166534" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="170" y1="40" x2="170" y2="125" stroke="#6b7280" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="210" y1="130" x2="210" y2="215" stroke="#6b7280" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="80" y1="35" x2="170" y2="80" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="170" y1="80" x2="210" y2="170" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="210" y1="170" x2="300" y2="215" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/><text x="176" y="52" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">normal</text><text x="10" y="24" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">incident ray</text><text x="40" y="110" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">air</text><text x="225" y="115" font-size="12" fill="#166534">glass block</text><text x="300" y="200" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">emergent ray</text><text x="150" y="72" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">i</text><text x="178" y="104" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">r</text></svg>

core.p: Light travels **more slowly in glass** than in air. When a ray enters glass at an angle, one side of the wavefront slows first, so the wave swings round and bends **towards the normal**. On leaving, it speeds up and bends **away from the normal**.
bullets: Angle of refraction in glass is **smaller** than the angle of incidence in air.
Larger angle of incidence gives larger angle of refraction, but the relationship is **not** a straight line through the origin with gradient 1.
A ray hitting the boundary **along the normal** (angle of incidence 0 degrees) does not change direction, but it still slows down.
The **frequency** of the wave does not change at a boundary; speed and wavelength change together (v = f x wavelength).
For a rectangular block, the emergent ray is **parallel** to the incident ray but shifted sideways.
Different colours refract by slightly different amounts, which is why a prism splits white light into a spectrum.

callouts.p: When a wave crosses a boundary its frequency is set by the source, so it does not change. Only the speed and wavelength change.

core.h: Transmission and absorption of light: coloured filters
core.p: When light meets a material it can be **transmitted** (passes through), **absorbed** (energy taken in by the material) or **reflected**. Coloured filters transmit only some wavelengths and absorb the rest.
bullets: A **red filter** transmits red light and absorbs other colours.
White light through a red filter comes out **red**; green light through a red filter is **absorbed**, so almost no light gets through.
An opaque object looks a certain colour because it **reflects** that colour and absorbs the others.
A white object reflects all colours; a black object absorbs all colours.
Different transparent materials transmit different amounts of light; a light sensor or light meter can measure the **intensity** transmitted.
Keep the source, distance and sensor fixed so only the material changes.

callouts.p: A filter cannot turn white light red by adding red. It **removes** (absorbs) the other colours, so only red is transmitted.

fig.cap: A red filter transmits red light and absorbs the other colours in white light.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="20" y="100" width="60" height="40" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#92400e"/><line x1="80" y1="112" x2="190" y2="112" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="80" y1="120" x2="190" y2="120" stroke="#16a34a" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="80" y1="128" x2="190" y2="128" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="3"/><rect x="190" y="80" width="16" height="80" fill="#fecaca" stroke="#991b1b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="206" y1="120" x2="340" y2="120" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="3"/><polygon points="340,114 352,120 340,126" fill="#dc2626"/><text x="20" y="90" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">lamp</text><text x="95" y="98" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">white light</text><text x="172" y="70" font-size="12" fill="#991b1b">red filter</text><text x="240" y="108" font-size="12" fill="#dc2626">red transmitted</text><text x="140" y="185" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">green and blue absorbed</text></svg>

core.h: Infrared emission and absorption by surfaces: method
core.p: All objects emit and absorb infrared radiation. A **Leslie cube** is a hollow metal cube with four different outer surfaces, filled with hot water so every face is at the same temperature.
bullets: Fill the Leslie cube with hot water from a kettle and place it on a heat-proof mat.
Point an **infrared detector** (or thermometer with a blackened bulb) at one face from a fixed distance.
Record the reading, then turn the cube and repeat for each face at the **same distance**.
Independent variable: **type of surface**. Dependent variable: **infrared detector reading**.
Control variables: water temperature (all faces share the same water), distance from detector, time of reading.
Take readings quickly, because the water cools over time.

callouts.p: Using one cube means all four surfaces are at the **same temperature**, so the only thing that changes between readings is the surface.

fig.cap: Leslie cube viewed from above. Each face has a different surface, and the infrared detector is held at the same distance from each face in turn.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="130" y="70" width="110" height="110" fill="#fecaca" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="130" y="64" width="110" height="8" fill="#1b2540"/><rect x="240" y="70" width="8" height="110" fill="#cbd5e1" stroke="#475569"/><rect x="130" y="180" width="110" height="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#475569"/><rect x="122" y="70" width="8" height="110" fill="#475569"/><text x="153" y="130" font-size="12" fill="#991b1b">hot water</text><text x="145" y="54" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">matt black</text><text x="145" y="206" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">matt white</text><text x="20" y="130" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">shiny black</text><rect x="310" y="110" width="50" height="30" fill="#e9d5ff" stroke="#6b21a8"/><line x1="250" y1="125" x2="308" y2="125" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><text x="300" y="100" font-size="12" fill="#6b21a8">IR detector</text><text x="255" y="160" font-size="12" fill="#475569">shiny silver</text></svg>

core.p: The **matt black** surface gives the highest detector reading and the **shiny silver** surface the lowest. Dark, matt surfaces are the best emitters and the best absorbers of infrared; light, shiny surfaces are the poorest emitters and absorbers and the best reflectors.
bullets: Good emitters are also good absorbers; poor emitters are also poor absorbers (good reflectors).
Matt black surface: **best emitter**, best absorber.
Shiny silver surface: **worst emitter**, best reflector.
Applications: solar panels are painted black to absorb more infrared; kettles and teapots are shiny to emit less and stay hot longer.
Emergency foil blankets are shiny to reduce infrared emitted from the body.
An object at constant temperature absorbs and emits infrared at the **same rate**.

callouts.p: A surface that is a good **emitter** of infrared is also a good **absorber** of infrared.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to identify variables or say how to make an investigation valid. A **valid** test only changes the independent variable and measures the dependent variable.
bullets: **Independent variable**: the one you deliberately change.
**Dependent variable**: the one you measure.
**Control variables**: everything kept the same so the test is fair.
Repeat readings and calculate a **mean** to reduce the effect of random errors.
Identify **anomalous** results and repeat them rather than including them in a mean.
A **systematic error** (such as a protractor zero misaligned) shifts every reading by the same amount and is not reduced by repeating.

callouts.p: An investigation is valid if it measures what it is supposed to measure, with only the independent variable changed.

core.p: Ray experiments are limited mainly by how accurately the ray position can be marked and the angle measured.
bullets: **Wide ray**: makes it hard to find the centre; use a narrower slit.
**Crosses too close together**: a small marking error causes a large angle error; mark crosses far apart.
**Parallax** when reading the protractor: read at eye level, directly above the scale.
**Normal not at 90 degrees**: draw it carefully with a protractor or set square.
Block moved during the experiment: draw round it and check it stays inside the outline.
For infrared, **background radiation** or a draught can affect readings; keep conditions constant.

callouts.p: A typical protractor has a resolution of 1 degree, so angle readings should be recorded to the nearest degree.

core.p: Results go in a table with the independent variable in the first column and units in the headings. For angle data, a graph shows the pattern clearly.
bullets: Table headings with units, for example **angle of incidence / degrees**.
Plot the **independent variable on the x-axis** and the dependent variable on the y-axis.
Draw a line or curve of best fit, not dot to dot.
Reflection: straight line through the origin, so angle of reflection is **directly proportional** to (equal to) angle of incidence.
Refraction: angle of refraction increases with angle of incidence but is always smaller, and the graph **curves**.
For infrared, a **bar chart** is used because the type of surface is a categoric variable.

callouts.p: Use a bar chart when the independent variable is **categoric** (type of surface, colour of filter); use a line graph when it is **continuous** (angle).

analogy.p: Imagine a row of marchers walking at an angle from a road onto a muddy field. The marchers who reach the mud first slow down while the others are still on the road at full speed, so the whole row swings round and changes direction towards the normal. This is refraction. If they walk straight on (along the normal), everyone hits the mud at once, slows together and keeps going straight. The analogy breaks down because light is not made of separate people, it needs no medium to travel through, and its frequency is fixed by the source, whereas marchers could change their step rate.

terms.d: A line drawn at 90 degrees to a surface at the point where a ray meets it; all angles are measured from it.
The angle between the incident ray and the normal.
The angle between the reflected ray and the normal.
The angle between the refracted ray and the normal.
The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
The change in direction of a wave as it crosses a boundary between media, due to a change in speed.
Reflection from a smooth surface in a single direction, producing a clear image.
Reflection from a rough surface where rays scatter in many directions.
When a wave passes through a material.
When a material takes in the energy of a wave.
A transparent material that transmits only certain colours (wavelengths) of light and absorbs the rest.
A hollow metal cube with different outer surfaces, filled with hot water, used to compare infrared emission.
Electromagnetic radiation emitted by all objects; hotter objects emit more.
A lamp in a box with a slit that produces a narrow beam of light.
The variable that is deliberately changed in an investigation.
The variable that is measured in an investigation.
Unpredictable variation in readings, reduced by repeating and taking a mean.

mistakes.w: Measuring the angle from the mirror or block surface.
mistakes.r: Angles are measured from the normal.

mistakes.w: Light bends away from the normal when it enters glass.
mistakes.r: Light slows down entering glass and bends towards the normal.

mistakes.w: Light speeds up when it enters glass.
mistakes.r: Light slows down in glass because glass is optically denser.

mistakes.w: The frequency changes when light is refracted.
mistakes.r: Frequency stays the same; speed and wavelength change.

mistakes.w: A ray along the normal is not refracted, so its speed does not change.
mistakes.r: It does not change direction, but its speed and wavelength still change.

mistakes.w: A red filter turns white light red by adding red.
mistakes.r: A red filter transmits red light and absorbs the other colours.

mistakes.w: Shiny surfaces are the best emitters because they look bright.
mistakes.r: Matt black surfaces are the best emitters and absorbers; shiny silver surfaces are the worst.

mistakes.w: Repeating readings removes systematic error.
mistakes.r: Repeating reduces random error; systematic error needs the method or equipment corrected.

mistakes.w: Drawing a line graph for type of surface.
mistakes.r: Type of surface is categoric, so a bar chart is used.

exam.q: State the law of reflection.
model: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection (measured from the normal).
exam.tip: Say both angles, and mention the normal for safety.

exam.q: Define the normal in a ray diagram.
model: A line at 90 degrees (perpendicular) to the surface at the point where the ray hits.
exam.tip: Use the word perpendicular or 90 degrees.

exam.q: A student shines a ray of light into a glass block. Explain why the ray changes direction.
model: Light slows down when it enters glass.
One side of the wavefront slows before the other, so the ray bends towards the normal.
exam.tip: Change in speed is the key mark; direction change follows from it.

exam.q: State what happens to the speed, wavelength and frequency of light as it passes from air into glass.
model: Speed decreases.
Wavelength decreases.
Frequency stays the same.
exam.tip: One mark for each quantity; frequency never changes at a boundary.

exam.q: Describe how a student could investigate the law of reflection using a plane mirror and a ray box.
model: Draw a line, place the mirror along it and draw a normal at 90 degrees.
Shine a narrow ray at the mirror where the normal meets it.
Mark incident and reflected rays with crosses and join them with a ruler.
Measure both angles from the normal with a protractor and repeat for different angles of incidence.
exam.tip: Include the normal, the protractor and repeating for different angles.

exam.q: Suggest two ways a student could improve the accuracy of measuring angles in a refraction experiment.
model: Use a narrower ray.
Mark crosses far apart along the ray / read the protractor at eye level.
exam.tip: Give specific practical improvements, not just 'be more careful'.

exam.q: White light is shone through a green filter. State and explain what colour light passes through.
model: Green light.
The filter transmits green and absorbs all other colours.
exam.tip: Use the words transmits and absorbs.

exam.q: Red light is shone through a blue filter. Explain what is observed.
model: Little or no light passes through / it appears dark.
The blue filter absorbs red light and only transmits blue, and there is no blue in red light.
exam.tip: Filters cannot create a colour that is not already present.

exam.q: A student uses a Leslie cube to compare infrared emitted by four surfaces. Name the independent variable, the dependent variable and two control variables.
model: Independent: type of surface.
Dependent: infrared detector reading.
Control: distance from detector to surface.
Control: temperature of the water / same time after filling.
exam.tip: Control variables must be things the student can actually keep the same.

exam.q: Explain why a Leslie cube is used rather than four separate containers.
model: All four surfaces are heated by the same water.
So all surfaces are at the same temperature, making it a fair test.
exam.tip: Link 'same water' to 'same temperature'.

exam.q: Describe and explain how a student could use a rectangular glass block to investigate how the angle of refraction depends on the angle of incidence. Include how results should be analysed.
model: Place the block on paper, draw round it and draw a normal at the point of entry.
Shine a narrow ray from a ray box at a measured angle of incidence.
Mark the path of the ray in and out with crosses, remove the block and join the points.
Measure the angle of refraction inside the block from the normal with a protractor.
Repeat for a range of angles of incidence and repeat each to calculate a mean.
Plot angle of refraction against angle of incidence; refraction angle is always smaller, because light slows down in glass and bends towards the normal.
exam.tip: For 6 marks include method, control of error, analysis and a physics explanation.

worked.q: A student measures the angle of reflection three times for an angle of incidence of 40 degrees: 39, 41 and 40 degrees. Calculate the mean and comment on whether the law of reflection is supported.
steps: The mean equals the angle of incidence.
The spread of 1 degree either side is due to random error such as ray width.
worked.ans: Mean angle of reflection = 40 degrees, which equals the angle of incidence, so the law of reflection is supported.

worked.q: A ray of light hits a glass block at an angle of incidence of 0 degrees. Describe what happens to the ray as it enters the block and explain why.
steps: An angle of incidence of 0 degrees means the ray travels along the normal.
The whole wavefront reaches the boundary at the same time.
The whole wavefront slows down together, so no side gets ahead of the other.
The ray therefore does not change direction, but its speed and wavelength decrease.
worked.ans: The ray passes straight through without bending, but it slows down and its wavelength decreases; its frequency is unchanged.

worked.q: Leslie cube results: matt black 82 units, shiny black 70, matt white 45, shiny silver 21. Use the data to state a conclusion and give one everyday application.
steps: Highest reading is matt black, lowest is shiny silver.
Dark surfaces emit more infrared than light surfaces; matt surfaces emit more than shiny ones.
Good emitters are also good absorbers.
Application: solar water panels are painted matt black to absorb as much infrared as possible.
worked.ans: Matt black is the best emitter and shiny silver the worst; dark, matt surfaces emit (and absorb) the most infrared, which is why solar panels are matt black.
